title: CompTIA A+ Core 1
realWorldValue: The 220-1201 is the first of two exams required for the CompTIA A+ certification, the long-standing entry credential for IT support roles. It validates foundational skills across mobile devices, networking, hardware, virtualisation and cloud, and hardware/network troubleshooting, making it the typical first certification for help desk technicians, field service engineers, and junior IT support staff.

skills: 1.1: Given a scenario, monitor mobile device hardware and use appropriate replacement techniques.
questions.question:
During routine checks, a technician examines a two-year-old business laptop that powers off unexpectedly when unplugged, even at a reported 60% charge. The battery health utility shows the design capacity is 56 Wh but the full-charge capacity has dropped to 18 Wh, with 412 cycles logged. The chassis around the battery bay is slightly raised and the trackpad has started clicking unevenly.

Which component should the technician replace?

choices.text: The internal lithium-ion battery, because it is swollen and has lost most of its usable capacity.
choices.explanation: Reduced full-charge capacity, high cycle count, and chassis bulging are classic signs of a failing, swollen battery.

choices.text: The DC jack and charging board, since power delivery appears unstable when running on battery.
choices.explanation: A faulty DC jack would affect charging while plugged in, not runtime on battery.

choices.text: The system board, because the power management IC is misreporting the charge level.
choices.explanation: Misreported charge alone would not cause physical bulging or capacity loss to a third of design.

choices.text: The trackpad assembly, since uneven clicking can indicate a power-related ground fault.
choices.explanation: The trackpad symptom is a consequence of the swollen battery pressing upward, not its cause.

questions.tip: Consider the combination of physical and electrical symptoms together.
questions.explanation:
A swollen battery is both an electrical and physical hazard.

**Why it works:** Lithium-ion cells lose capacity over hundreds of cycles and can outgas, causing the pack to swell and push on surrounding components like the trackpad.

**Why the others don't work:**
- DC jack: would affect charging on AC, not unplugged runtime.
- System board: a reporting bug would not cause physical bulging or capacity collapse.
- Trackpad: its symptom is downstream of the swelling battery underneath.

skills: 1.1: Given a scenario, monitor mobile device hardware and use appropriate replacement techniques.
questions.question:
A user reports that their laptop's Wi-Fi connection works perfectly when sitting at a desk near the router but drops repeatedly when carrying the device around the office. The technician recently replaced the LCD panel after a screen crack. Other laptops in the same areas hold their connection without issue.

What is the MOST likely cause of the intermittent wireless behaviour?

choices.text: The Wi-Fi antenna leads routed through the display hinge were not reconnected to the wireless card after the screen replacement.
choices.explanation: Laptop Wi-Fi antennas typically run up through the hinge into the lid, and reduced range after screen work points to disconnected or pinched antenna cables.

choices.text: The replacement LCD panel is drawing excess current and starving the wireless card of power.
choices.explanation: LCD panels and Wi-Fi cards are on separate rails, and panel current draw does not cause range loss.

choices.text: The wireless card firmware needs reflashing after the display was replaced.
choices.explanation: Display replacement does not alter Wi-Fi card firmware or its configuration.

choices.text: The 802.11 driver in the operating system has reverted to a legacy power-saving mode.
choices.explanation: Power-saving mode would behave consistently regardless of physical position relative to the router.

questions.tip: Think about where the antennas physically live in most laptop designs.
questions.explanation:
Wi-Fi antennas typically sit in the lid for better line of sight.

**Why it works:** During screen replacement, antenna leads run through the hinge to the wireless card. If they are not reseated correctly, signal strength drops sharply with distance.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Power starvation: LCD and Wi-Fi share no rail that would cause this.
- Firmware: not touched by panel work.
- Power-saving: would not depend on physical distance from the AP.

skills: 1.1: Given a scenario, monitor mobile device hardware and use appropriate replacement techniques.
questions.question:
An accountant's ultrabook has begun freezing during heavy spreadsheet work, and the Resource Monitor shows committed memory pegged at 99% with constant pagefile activity. The laptop has a single SODIMM slot populated with an 8 GB module, and the service manual lists a maximum supported capacity of 32 GB.

Which upgrade is the MOST appropriate next step?

choices.text: Replace the existing 8 GB SODIMM with a single higher-capacity SODIMM that matches the laptop's supported speed and form factor.
choices.explanation: A single-slot laptop can only be upgraded by swapping the existing module for a larger one of the correct type.

choices.text: Add a second SODIMM in dual-channel configuration alongside the existing 8 GB module.
choices.explanation: The chassis has only one SODIMM slot, so dual-channel installation is not possible.

choices.text: Install a DDR5 desktop DIMM after confirming the BIOS supports the newer standard.
choices.explanation: Laptops use SODIMM, not full-size DIMM, and form factor is not BIOS-selectable.

choices.text: Replace the SSD with a larger NVMe drive to expand pagefile headroom.
choices.explanation: A bigger pagefile masks rather than fixes a RAM shortfall and does not improve responsiveness.

questions.tip: Match the physical and electrical constraints of the platform.
questions.explanation:
Single-slot laptops force a swap rather than an add.

**Why it works:** With only one SODIMM slot and a 32 GB ceiling, replacing the 8 GB module with a 16 or 32 GB SODIMM of the supported speed resolves the shortage.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Second SODIMM: there is no second slot.
- Desktop DIMM: wrong form factor for a laptop.
- Larger SSD: pagefile is not a substitute for physical RAM.

questions.question:
Following a coffee spill, a user reports that the letters E, R, and T on their laptop register multiple characters or fail to register on each press. Other keys function normally, the trackpad is responsive, and external USB keyboards work without issue. The device is under a depot warranty that excludes liquid damage.

Which replacement action should the technician take?

choices.text: Replace the entire laptop keyboard assembly, since individual membrane layers cannot be repaired in the field.
choices.explanation: Laptop keyboards are sealed assemblies; localized liquid damage to membranes requires full keyboard replacement.

choices.text: Pry off and clean the affected keycaps, then reseat them on the existing scissor mechanisms.
choices.explanation: Surface cleaning will not restore membrane traces that have been corroded or shorted by liquid.

choices.text: Replace the system board, since the keyboard controller is integrated into the chipset.
choices.explanation: The keyboard controller is rarely the failure point when only a few adjacent keys are affected after a spill.

choices.text: Reinstall the keyboard driver and run a key remapping utility for the affected keys.
choices.explanation: Software remediation cannot fix physical membrane damage and would not restore reliable input.

questions.tip: Consider what level of granularity is actually serviceable on modern laptops.
questions.explanation:
Modern laptop keyboards are not designed for component-level repair.

**Why it works:** The keyboard is a sealed membrane assembly; once liquid damages the traces, the whole unit must be swapped.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Keycap cleaning: cosmetic only, doesn't reach damaged membranes.
- System board: external keyboards work, so the controller path is fine.
- Driver/remap: software cannot restore broken electrical contacts.

questions.question:
The hardware refresh team is documenting the privacy features available on a new fleet of corporate laptops aimed at executives who travel frequently. Procurement has asked for two physical privacy or security components that can be specified at order time rather than added later.

Which TWO components should be listed?

choices.text: An integrated fingerprint reader for biometric sign-in at the device.
choices.explanation: Fingerprint readers are a common biometric authentication option built into the chassis or power button.

choices.text: A mechanical webcam privacy shutter built into the bezel.
choices.explanation: A built-in shutter physically blocks the camera lens, providing a tamper-evident privacy assurance.

choices.text: A USB-attached HSM dongle that issues certificates on demand.
choices.explanation: An external dongle is not a built-in component specified at the device order.

choices.text: A software password manager preinstalled by the OEM.
choices.explanation: Preinstalled software is not a physical privacy or security component.

choices.text: A removable microSD card for encrypted storage offload.
choices.explanation: MicroSD storage is an accessory, not a privacy or biometric feature integrated into the chassis.

questions.tip: Focus on components physically integrated into the laptop hardware.
questions.explanation:
Physical privacy and security components are built into the device chassis at manufacture.

**Why it works:** Fingerprint readers and webcam shutters are both integral hardware that can be ticked as build options. They protect authentication and visual privacy respectively.

**Why the others don't work:**
- USB HSM: external accessory, not integrated.
- OEM software: not a physical component.
- microSD: storage option, not a privacy or biometric feature.

questions.question: Match each laptop symptom to the internal component most likely responsible.

slots.label: Video calls show the user but no audio is transmitted to participants, even with a fresh OS install.
Boot fails with a SMART warning and slow read speeds reported by the OS.
Webcam image appears as a black square in every conferencing app.
Bluetooth and Wi-Fi both disappear from device manager after a knock to the chassis.

choices.text: Internal microphone module
choices.explanation: Audio capture failure that survives an OS reinstall points to the mic hardware or its cable.

choices.text: Solid-state drive nearing failure
choices.explanation: SMART warnings and degraded read performance indicate the storage device is failing.

choices.text: Camera or webcam module
choices.explanation: A consistent black image across applications points to the camera module or its ribbon cable.

choices.text: Combined wireless card (Wi-Fi and Bluetooth)
choices.explanation: Most laptops combine Wi-Fi and Bluetooth on one M.2 card; an unseated card removes both radios at once.

questions.tip: Pair each symptom with the single component whose failure best explains it.
questions.explanation: Each symptom maps to a distinct serviceable module inside a typical laptop. Recognising the signature failure of each speeds up replacement decisions.

skills: 1.2: Compare and contrast accessories and connectivity options for mobile devices.
questions.question:
During a desk rollout, the IT team is equipping hot-desking workstations so that any visiting employee can plug their corporate laptop into a single connector and immediately drive two external displays, charge the laptop, and connect to the wired network and peripheral hub. The chosen solution must use one cable per laptop and adapt to multiple laptop brands.

Which device should the team specify?

choices.text: A USB-C docking station that supports DisplayPort alt mode, Power Delivery, and Ethernet over a single host cable.
choices.explanation: A USB-C dock provides charging, video, USB, and Ethernet through one connector across vendor-agnostic laptops.

choices.text: A proprietary port replicator designed for a single laptop family.
choices.explanation: Port replicators are typically tied to one vendor's connector, breaking multi-brand support.

choices.text: A powered USB-A hub combined with a separate HDMI splitter at each desk.
choices.explanation: A USB-A hub cannot deliver enough power to charge a laptop and lacks display alt mode.

choices.text: A Bluetooth keyboard-mouse combo paired with each visitor's laptop on arrival.
choices.explanation: Bluetooth peripherals do not address video, charging, or wired networking requirements.

questions.tip: Look for the option that consolidates power, video, and data on one connector.
questions.explanation:
A USB-C dock is the only option meeting all four requirements over one cable.

**Why it works:** USB-C carries DisplayPort alt mode for monitors, Power Delivery for charging, and tunneled USB and Ethernet for peripherals and network.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Port replicator: vendor-locked.
- USB-A hub: no charging or alt-mode video.
- Bluetooth combo: only addresses input, not display or power.

skills: 1.2: Compare and contrast accessories and connectivity options for mobile devices.
questions.question:
Field engineers staying at a hotel report that the conference room Wi-Fi is unusable but their corporate mobile phones have strong 5G signal. They need to bring two laptops online for a customer demo within the next ten minutes and the phones have unlimited data plans.

Which connectivity option should they use?

choices.text: Enable the mobile hotspot feature on one phone and join both laptops to its Wi-Fi network.
choices.explanation: Mobile hotspot shares the phone's cellular connection over Wi-Fi to nearby devices.

choices.text: Pair the laptops to the phone over NFC and let the OS negotiate a data session.
choices.explanation: NFC is for short bursts of data such as pairing initiation or payment, not internet sharing.

choices.text: Pair both laptops to the phone over Bluetooth and use file transfer to relay HTTP traffic.
choices.explanation: Bluetooth file transfer is not a routing mechanism and would not carry general internet traffic.

choices.text: Connect a single laptop to the phone via Lightning cable and share the screen to the second laptop.
choices.explanation: Screen sharing does not give the second laptop independent internet access.

questions.tip: Identify the connectivity method designed to share cellular data with multiple clients.
questions.explanation:
Mobile hotspot turns the phone into a small access point.

**Why it works:** The phone broadcasts a Wi-Fi SSID backed by its cellular data, allowing multiple clients to use the connection simultaneously.

**Why the others don't work:**
- NFC: only centimetres of range and minimal throughput.
- Bluetooth file transfer: not an internet path.
- Lightning screen share: doesn't network the second laptop.

skills: 1.2: Compare and contrast accessories and connectivity options for mobile devices.
questions.question:
A retail customer has an older Android phone that uses a small trapezoidal port for charging and data. Their charger has failed and they are looking at a wall of replacement cables in the shop, each labelled with a different connector type.

Which cable should the technician recommend?

choices.text: A microUSB cable.
choices.explanation: MicroUSB has the trapezoidal shape that older Android handsets used as their standard charging and data port.

choices.text: A Lightning cable.
choices.explanation: Lightning is an Apple proprietary connector and does not fit Android handsets.

choices.text: A USB-C cable.
choices.explanation: USB-C is reversible and oval, not the trapezoidal shape described.

choices.text: A miniUSB cable.
choices.explanation: MiniUSB is larger and shaped differently, used mainly on older cameras and external drives.

questions.tip: Picture the connector shape associated with each name.
questions.explanation:
MicroUSB was the dominant Android port for many years.

**Why it works:** Its small trapezoidal plug matches the customer's description and predates USB-C on most Android devices.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Lightning: Apple only.
- USB-C: oval and reversible.
- MiniUSB: larger and obsolete for phones.

skills: 1.2: Compare and contrast accessories and connectivity options for mobile devices.
questions.question:
An architect wants to annotate building plans directly on a tablet during site visits, using pressure-sensitive handwriting and palm rejection. They already own a high-end tablet that supports active digitizer input. Procurement asks the technician what to order.

Which accessory best meets the requirement?

choices.text: An active stylus compatible with the tablet's digitizer protocol.
choices.explanation: An active stylus communicates pressure and palm-rejection data with a compatible digitizer.

choices.text: A capacitive rubber-tip passive pen.
choices.explanation: Passive pens cannot report pressure levels or trigger palm rejection.

choices.text: An external drawing pad that connects over USB.
choices.explanation: A separate drawing pad does not let the user annotate directly on the tablet's screen.

choices.text: A Bluetooth presenter remote with a laser pointer.
choices.explanation: A presenter remote provides clicks, not handwriting input.

questions.tip: Match the input device to the digitizer feature set the screen supports.
questions.explanation:
Active styluses pair with digitizer tablets to deliver pressure and tilt data.

**Why it works:** A compatible active stylus unlocks pressure sensitivity and palm rejection at the screen surface, ideal for annotation.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Passive pen: no pressure or palm data.
- External drawing pad: input goes to a separate surface.
- Presenter remote: not a writing instrument.

skills: 1.2: Compare and contrast accessories and connectivity options for mobile devices.
questions.question:
Following a hybrid working policy, employees need to connect their personal Bluetooth wireless headsets to a corporate laptop for daily calls. The IT helpdesk is writing a quick-start guide that lists the TWO steps that must be performed at the laptop side to make the headset usable.

Which TWO steps should the guide include?

choices.text: Enable Bluetooth on the laptop and put the radio into discoverable or pairing mode.
choices.explanation: The laptop must have Bluetooth enabled and be ready to discover the headset before it can be paired.

choices.text: Pair the headset and then set it as the default audio input and output device in the OS sound settings.
choices.explanation: After pairing, the OS must be told to route audio through the headset rather than internal speakers.

choices.text: Install the manufacturer's USB receiver into a free USB-A port.
choices.explanation: Bluetooth headsets do not require a vendor USB receiver; that describes proprietary RF dongles.

choices.text: Tether the laptop to a mobile hotspot so the headset can use the cellular channel.
choices.explanation: Tethering provides internet access and is unrelated to local audio routing.

choices.text: Tap the headset against the laptop's NFC zone to negotiate a Wi-Fi Direct session.
choices.explanation: Headset audio uses Bluetooth profiles, not Wi-Fi Direct, even when NFC speeds up pairing.

questions.tip: Think about both the connection and the audio routing on the host device.
questions.explanation:
Bluetooth audio needs the radio enabled and the OS routing configured.

**Why it works:** Putting the laptop into pairing mode allows discovery, and setting the headset as the default device tells the OS to send audio to it after pairing.

**Why the others don't work:**
- USB receiver: wrong technology family.
- Tethering: unrelated to audio.
- NFC to Wi-Fi Direct: not how Bluetooth headsets work.

skills: 1.2: Compare and contrast accessories and connectivity options for mobile devices.
questions.question: Match each mobile connectivity scenario to the most appropriate connection method.

slots.label: Tap-to-pay at a contactless payment terminal
Sharing a phone's cellular data with a laptop over a physical cable
Connecting a wireless keyboard to a tablet across a few metres
Charging and driving an external monitor from a modern laptop over one cable

choices.text: Near-field communication
choices.explanation: NFC operates at a few centimetres and is the basis for contactless payments.

choices.text: USB tethering
choices.explanation: USB tethering connects the phone to the laptop over a cable and shares the cellular link.

choices.text: Bluetooth
choices.explanation: Bluetooth supports low-power peripherals such as keyboards over short ranges.

choices.text: USB-C with Power Delivery and DisplayPort alt mode
choices.explanation: USB-C alt mode carries DisplayPort signal while Power Delivery handles charging on the same cable.

questions.tip: Match each scenario to the method whose range, throughput, and signalling fit best.
questions.explanation: Each connection method has a niche defined by range, throughput, and signalling. Knowing the typical use case for NFC, tethering, Bluetooth, and USB-C is core to mobile device support.

questions.question:
A user travelling abroad has bought a local prepaid plan but does not want to remove the physical SIM that holds their home number. Their handset is dual-SIM capable, supports both physical and embedded SIMs, and was sold unlocked. They want to keep both lines active and pick which one places outbound calls.

Which approach should the technician walk them through?

choices.text: Activate the local carrier's eSIM profile in addition to the physical SIM, then select the preferred line for outbound calls in the dual-SIM settings.
choices.explanation: An eSIM lets the user add a second line digitally while keeping the home physical SIM in place and choose a default for calls.

choices.text: Swap the physical SIM for the local one and use call forwarding from the home number.
choices.explanation: This removes the home SIM and depends on forwarding being active, which doesn't meet the requirement to keep both lines on the device.

choices.text: Enable Wi-Fi calling only and disable the cellular radio entirely while abroad.
choices.explanation: Disabling cellular drops the home line completely and breaks the dual-SIM requirement.

choices.text: Tether the handset to a second device that holds the local SIM.
choices.explanation: Tethering doesn't make the local number callable from the original handset.

questions.tip: Identify the technology that lets a second carrier profile coexist with a physical SIM.
questions.explanation:
eSIM provisioning adds a second carrier profile without removing the physical SIM.

**Why it works:** Modern handsets allow dual-SIM operation by combining a physical SIM with an embedded SIM profile, and the user can pick the default line per service.

**Why the others don't work:**
- SIM swap: loses the home line.
- Wi-Fi calling only: disables cellular entirely.
- Tethering: doesn't bring the line into the handset.

skills: 1.3: Given a scenario, configure basic mobile device network connectivity and provide application support.
questions.question:
An employee using their personal phone under a BYOD scheme reports that the corporate mail app has stopped syncing while personal apps continue to work normally. The MDM console shows the device as compliant. They mention they recently changed the screen lock from a six-digit PIN to a four-digit one.

What is the MOST likely cause?

choices.text: The MDM policy enforces a minimum passcode complexity that the new four-digit PIN no longer satisfies, blocking corporate app access until it is corrected.
choices.explanation: MDM passcode policies commonly require a minimum length or complexity; falling below it blocks managed app access.

choices.text: The mail server has revoked the OAuth token because the device IMEI changed.
choices.explanation: Changing the screen lock does not alter the device IMEI.

choices.text: The personal Apple ID or Google account was signed out by the new PIN.
choices.explanation: Changing the screen PIN does not sign the user out of their personal cloud account.

choices.text: The mobile network has throttled the device after exceeding its data cap.
choices.explanation: Throttling would affect personal apps too, not selectively the corporate mailbox.

questions.tip: Consider what a BYOD policy can require independently of personal settings.
questions.explanation:
MDM enforces baseline security on managed apps even in BYOD.

**Why it works:** When the device drops below the required passcode complexity, the MDM agent gates access to corporate apps until the user restores compliance.

**Why the others don't work:**
- IMEI/OAuth: PIN length doesn't change IMEI.
- Cloud sign-out: not triggered by PIN changes.
- Cap throttling: would affect everything, not just one app.

questions.question:
During a hike with no cellular coverage, a user opens a topographic mapping app and is surprised that their precise position still appears on the map even though their phone shows no bars and is in airplane mode with Wi-Fi off but location enabled.

Which service is providing the position fix?

choices.text: The phone's GPS receiver, which obtains a fix directly from navigation satellites without needing the cellular network.
choices.explanation: GPS works from satellite signals and does not require any cellular or Wi-Fi link to obtain a position.

choices.text: Cellular tower triangulation through the carrier.
choices.explanation: Airplane mode disables the cellular radio and there is no signal anyway.

choices.text: Wi-Fi positioning against a database of nearby SSIDs.
choices.explanation: Wi-Fi is switched off, so no scan data is available.

choices.text: The MDM agent reporting an enterprise-pushed coordinate.
choices.explanation: MDM does not provide the device with a current location; it consumes it.

questions.tip: Identify which of the location sources is independent of any infrastructure connection.
questions.explanation:
GPS is a receive-only satellite system.

**Why it works:** As long as the GPS receiver can see the sky, it computes a position from satellite signals with no need for cellular or Wi-Fi.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Cellular triangulation: needs a live cellular link.
- Wi-Fi positioning: needs Wi-Fi scanning enabled.
- MDM: does not feed location back to the device.

questions.question:
Helpdesk has received a ticket from a user trying to pair a new car infotainment system with their phone. The car displays a six-digit code on its screen and asks the driver to confirm. The phone shows the same six digits and offers Pair and Cancel buttons.

What should the user do next to complete the pairing?

choices.text: Confirm that the two displayed codes match and tap Pair on the phone.
choices.explanation: Numeric comparison pairing requires the user to verify both displays show the same value before accepting.

choices.text: Enter the phone's lock-screen PIN into the car infotainment keypad.
choices.explanation: The screen lock PIN is unrelated to Bluetooth pairing and would not be accepted.

choices.text: Cancel pairing and switch the car system to NFC mode instead.
choices.explanation: Numeric comparison is the expected flow; switching modes is unnecessary.

choices.text: Forget the car from previous devices on the phone, then re-scan.
choices.explanation: Forgetting an unpaired device offers no benefit and disrupts the current attempt.

questions.tip: Recognise the Bluetooth pairing flow being described.
questions.explanation:
This is Bluetooth numeric comparison pairing.

**Why it works:** Both devices generate the same six-digit code from the pairing exchange; confirming that they match completes secure pairing.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Lock PIN: unrelated to Bluetooth.
- NFC mode: not required, the flow is already underway.
- Forget device: nothing to forget yet.

questions.question:
A new salesperson has been issued a corporate phone and asks the helpdesk to make sure their meetings and contact list appear on the device, alongside cloud storage for shared documents. The helpdesk wants to identify which sync categories cover the request.

Which THREE data types should be enabled for synchronization?

choices.text: Calendar entries from the corporate mail account.
choices.explanation: Meeting visibility on the device depends on calendar synchronization with the mail account.

choices.text: Contacts from the corporate directory.
choices.explanation: Phone numbers and addresses appear on the handset when contact sync is enabled.

choices.text: Corporate cloud storage for shared documents.
choices.explanation: Cloud storage sync gives mobile access to shared files referenced in meetings.

choices.text: Wallpapers and ringtone packs from the OEM store.
choices.explanation: Personalization assets are not part of business data sync.

choices.text: Mobile carrier billing statements pushed via SMS.
choices.explanation: Carrier billing is unrelated to corporate productivity sync.

choices.text: Web browser history from a personal account.
choices.explanation: Personal browsing history is outside the corporate sync scope.

questions.tip: Focus on the business data categories the user actually asked for.
questions.explanation:
The helpdesk should turn on the sync types tied to the stated business needs.

**Why it works:** Calendar, contacts, and cloud storage sync collectively cover meetings, people, and shared documents requested by the salesperson.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Wallpapers: cosmetic only.
- Carrier SMS: not business sync.
- Browser history: personal scope.

questions.question: Arrange the following steps in the correct order to pair a wireless Bluetooth speaker with a smartphone for the first time.

choices.text: Enable Bluetooth on the smartphone and open the Bluetooth settings screen.
choices.explanation: The phone radio must be on and the settings open before pairing can begin.

choices.text: Put the speaker into pairing mode so it becomes discoverable.
choices.explanation: The speaker must advertise itself before the phone can find it.

choices.text: Select the speaker from the list of nearby devices on the phone and confirm or enter the PIN if prompted.
choices.explanation: Selecting the device initiates the pairing exchange, which may require a confirmation or PIN.

choices.text: Play audio through the speaker to test that the connection is working.
choices.explanation: Playing audio verifies that pairing succeeded and the speaker is the active output.

questions.tip: Think about which side must be ready before the other can act.
questions.explanation: Each step depends on the previous one. The host radio must be enabled, the peripheral must be discoverable, the user must select and authenticate the device, and finally connectivity is verified by use.

skills: 2.1: Compare and contrast Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and User Datagram Protocol (UDP) ports, protocols, and their purposes.
questions.question:
A help-desk technician is troubleshooting a remote office worker who needs to manage a Linux server over an encrypted command-line session. The user reports that the legacy plaintext terminal protocol is blocked at the corporate firewall, and the security team has standardised on encrypted equivalents. The technician needs to open the correct outbound port on the host-based firewall.

Which port should the technician permit for the encrypted remote shell?

choices.text: TCP port 22 for SSH, which provides an encrypted interactive shell and replaces the plaintext alternative on Linux servers.
choices.explanation: SSH on TCP 22 is the standard encrypted replacement for Telnet for command-line server management.

choices.text: TCP port 23 for Telnet, opened only on the outbound interface so that the plaintext session never reaches the public internet.
choices.explanation: Telnet is unencrypted regardless of which interface it traverses and is the protocol being blocked by policy.

choices.text: TCP port 3389 for RDP, configured for a text-only console mode that limits bandwidth across the wide area link.
choices.explanation: RDP is the Microsoft graphical remote desktop protocol and is not used for shell management of a Linux server.

choices.text: TCP port 443 for HTTPS, tunnelling the terminal session inside the browser's TLS channel to the server.
choices.explanation: HTTPS on 443 is for web traffic, not for an interactive command-line shell to a Linux server.

questions.tip: Consider which port number the standard encrypted command-line management protocol uses.
questions.explanation:
Linux servers are managed remotely over an encrypted shell that listens on a well-known TCP port.

**Why it works:** SSH operates on TCP 22 and provides an authenticated, encrypted interactive terminal session that has long since replaced Telnet.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Telnet on 23: plaintext and the protocol explicitly being phased out.
- RDP on 3389: a graphical Windows remote desktop protocol, not a Linux shell.
- HTTPS on 443: a web traffic port, not a remote shell port.

skills: 2.1: Compare and contrast Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and User Datagram Protocol (UDP) ports, protocols, and their purposes.
questions.question:
During an office relocation, a technician sets up a new client workstation and notices the machine cannot reach any internal servers by hostname, even though pinging by IP address works. The other workstations on the subnet resolve names correctly, and the local firewall has no outbound DNS rule yet. The technician needs to allow the resolver to query the corporate name server.

Which port and transport should the firewall rule allow for standard name resolution queries?

choices.text: UDP port 53 outbound to the corporate DNS server, which carries standard resolver queries.
choices.explanation: Standard DNS lookups use UDP 53 because the queries and responses fit in a single small datagram.

choices.text: TCP port 25 outbound to the corporate DNS server, matching the connection-oriented nature of name lookups.
choices.explanation: Port 25 is SMTP for mail transfer and is unrelated to name resolution.

choices.text: UDP port 67 outbound to the corporate DNS server, which is the standard port for client-issued lookups.
choices.explanation: UDP 67 is used by DHCP servers, not for DNS resolution.

choices.text: TCP port 110 outbound to the corporate DNS server, which provides reliable delivery of the response record.
choices.explanation: TCP 110 is POP3 mail retrieval and is not used for DNS queries.

questions.tip: Recall which transport protocol is preferred for short request/response name lookups.
questions.explanation:
Standard DNS queries are short and benefit from the low overhead of a connectionless transport.

**Why it works:** DNS clients send resolver queries to UDP 53 because each lookup is a single small request and reply, with TCP 53 reserved for larger transfers such as zone transfers.

**Why the others don't work:**
- TCP 25: SMTP, unrelated to name resolution.
- UDP 67: DHCP server port, not DNS.
- TCP 110: POP3 mail retrieval port.

skills: 2.1: Compare and contrast Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and User Datagram Protocol (UDP) ports, protocols, and their purposes.
questions.question:
The desktop support team has rolled out a new file server and users need to access mapped drives from their Windows workstations. The Windows firewall on the server is currently blocking all inbound traffic, and the network team has asked for a single port to be opened for the file-sharing protocol used natively by modern Windows clients.

Which port should be opened on the file server's firewall?

choices.text: TCP port 445 for SMB, which carries modern Windows file and printer sharing traffic directly over TCP/IP.
choices.explanation: Modern Windows file sharing uses SMB directly over TCP 445 without the legacy NetBIOS layer.

choices.text: TCP port 21 for FTP, providing standard file transfer access between Windows clients and the server.
choices.explanation: FTP is a separate file-transfer protocol and is not what Windows uses for mapped network drives.

choices.text: TCP port 389 for LDAP, which Windows uses to negotiate file-share access through directory services.
choices.explanation: LDAP is for directory queries to domain controllers, not for SMB file access.

choices.text: TCP port 143 for IMAP, allowing the file-sharing client to retrieve documents over an authenticated session.
choices.explanation: IMAP is a mailbox protocol for email retrieval, not file-share access.

questions.tip: Think about which port carries native Windows file-share traffic without legacy NetBIOS dependencies.
questions.explanation:
Windows file sharing now runs directly over TCP rather than relying on the older NetBIOS framing.

**Why it works:** SMB/CIFS uses TCP 445 to deliver file, printer, and named-pipe traffic between Windows hosts.

**Why the others don't work:**
- FTP 21: a separate file-transfer protocol, not used for mapped drives.
- LDAP 389: for directory lookups, not file shares.
- IMAP 143: for email retrieval.

skills: 2.1: Compare and contrast Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and User Datagram Protocol (UDP) ports, protocols, and their purposes.
questions.question:
An administrator is reviewing a packet capture from a VoIP gateway and notices that the real-time call audio streams use a connectionless transport with no retransmissions. A colleague asks why the engineers chose this transport instead of the connection-oriented one used by web traffic.

Which characteristic of UDP best explains its suitability for real-time voice traffic?

choices.text: UDP is connectionless and does not retransmit lost packets, which keeps latency low for time-sensitive audio.
choices.explanation: Real-time media tolerates small loss but cannot wait for retransmissions, so UDP's low overhead is preferred.

choices.text: UDP uses a three-way handshake that completes faster than TCP, giving call setup lower latency.
choices.explanation: UDP has no handshake at all; the handshake described is a TCP feature.

choices.text: UDP guarantees in-order delivery of packets, which keeps audio samples aligned at the receiver.
choices.explanation: UDP makes no ordering guarantees; that is one of the features TCP provides.

choices.text: UDP performs windowed flow control to throttle the sender when the receiver is busy.
choices.explanation: Flow control with sliding windows is a TCP feature, not a UDP one.

questions.tip: Focus on what UDP deliberately leaves out compared with TCP.
questions.explanation:
Real-time audio prefers a transport that minimises delay over one that guarantees reliability.

**Why it works:** UDP is connectionless with no retransmissions, acknowledgements, or ordering, so packets arrive with the lowest possible delay even if some are lost.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Handshake claim: UDP has no handshake.
- Ordering claim: UDP does not guarantee order.
- Flow control claim: windowed flow control is a TCP feature.

skills: 2.1: Compare and contrast Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and User Datagram Protocol (UDP) ports, protocols, and their purposes.
questions.question:
A small business has migrated to a new mail platform and the IT contractor is hardening the office firewall. Users retrieve mail through a client that keeps messages on the server so they can be read from multiple devices, and outgoing messages still flow through the existing on-premises relay. The contractor needs to permit the two ports the mail client uses.

Which TWO ports should be opened outbound to support the new configuration?

choices.text: TCP port 143 for IMAP to retrieve messages from the server while keeping them stored centrally.
choices.explanation: IMAP on 143 supports multi-device access by leaving messages on the server.

choices.text: TCP port 25 for SMTP to relay outgoing messages through the existing on-premises mail relay.
choices.explanation: SMTP on 25 is the standard transport for sending mail to a relay server.

choices.text: TCP port 110 for POP3 to download mail to each device and remove it from the server.
choices.explanation: POP3 conflicts with the multi-device requirement because it typically removes messages from the server.

choices.text: TCP port 53 for DNS to look up `MX` records used when delivering messages.
choices.explanation: DNS lookups happen automatically and are not the mail client's transport for messages.

choices.text: TCP port 3389 for RDP so administrators can manage the mailbox server remotely.
choices.explanation: RDP is unrelated to client mail retrieval or sending.

questions.tip: Match each requirement to the matching mail-protocol port.
questions.explanation:
Two separate protocols handle inbound and outbound mail traffic.

**Why it works:** IMAP on TCP 143 keeps the mailbox on the server, supporting access from multiple devices, while SMTP on TCP 25 carries outbound messages to the relay.

**Why the others don't work:**
- POP3 110: removes messages from the server, breaking multi-device access.
- DNS 53: a name-lookup transport, not a mail client transport.
- RDP 3389: administrative remote desktop, unrelated to mail flow.

skills: 2.1: Compare and contrast Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and User Datagram Protocol (UDP) ports, protocols, and their purposes.
questions.question: Match each standard port number to the protocol that uses it.

choices.text: HTTPS, encrypted web traffic to and from web servers
choices.explanation: HTTPS uses TCP 443 to wrap HTTP inside TLS.

choices.text: RDP, graphical remote desktop sessions to Windows hosts
choices.explanation: RDP uses TCP 3389 for the remote desktop session protocol.

choices.text: LDAP, directory lookups against a domain or directory service
choices.explanation: LDAP uses TCP 389 to query directory services such as Active Directory.

choices.text: DHCP, automatic IPv4 address allocation between client and server
choices.explanation: DHCP uses UDP 67 on the server and UDP 68 on the client.

questions.tip: Map each port number to the service most commonly bound to it in default configurations.
questions.explanation: Each port number is associated with a single well-known protocol at the application layer, and recognising those mappings is core knowledge for entry-level network troubleshooting.

skills: 2.2: Explain wireless networking technologies.
questions.question:
Following a complaint about poor wireless coverage in a warehouse with thick metal racking, a technician runs a site survey and finds that the existing 5 GHz access points cannot reach the far aisles. The supplied client devices are all dual-band but spend most of their time at distance from the nearest AP, and the team needs the longest practical range from the existing radios.

Which frequency band should the technician prioritise for new APs in the far aisles?

choices.text: The 2.4 GHz band, which has longer range and penetrates obstacles better than the higher bands.
choices.explanation: Lower-frequency signals propagate further and pass through walls and racking more readily.

choices.text: The 5 GHz band at 80 MHz channel width, since wider channels carry signal further into the warehouse.
choices.explanation: Wider channels reduce range and effective power per Hz, they do not extend coverage.

choices.text: The 6 GHz band, because the newer spectrum is uncongested and therefore reaches further than older bands.
choices.explanation: Less congestion does not increase propagation distance; 6 GHz has the shortest practical range of the three.

choices.text: Both 5 GHz and 6 GHz simultaneously, using band steering to maximise the reach of each client.
choices.explanation: Band steering can rebalance load but cannot extend the physical reach of higher-frequency radios.

questions.tip: Consider which wireless band offers the greatest propagation distance.
questions.explanation:
Lower-frequency wireless signals travel further and penetrate obstacles more effectively than higher-frequency ones.

**Why it works:** 2.4 GHz has longer wavelengths than 5 GHz or 6 GHz, giving it better range and obstacle penetration in cluttered industrial spaces.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Wider 5 GHz channels: actually reduce range due to lower power per subcarrier.
- 6 GHz: shortest range of the three bands.
- Band steering: redistributes clients, does not extend coverage.

skills: 2.2: Explain wireless networking technologies.
questions.question:
During a wireless refresh, a technician is configuring a new 2.4 GHz radio in a building shared with several other tenants. A Wi-Fi analyser shows heavy overlap on channels 3, 6, 9, and 11, and the technician wants to pick channels that do not overlap with one another so that nearby APs can coexist cleanly.

Which set of 2.4 GHz channels should the technician choose for non-overlapping operation?

choices.text: Channels 1, 6, and 11 across the three APs, which are the standard non-overlapping channels in the 2.4 GHz band.
choices.explanation: These three channels are spaced far enough apart that their 20 MHz channel widths do not overlap.

choices.text: Channels 2, 7, and 12, spaced five apart to guarantee non-overlap across the band.
choices.explanation: Five-channel spacing in 2.4 GHz still overlaps because each 20 MHz channel occupies more than five channel numbers.

choices.text: Channels 36, 40, and 44, since UNII-1 provides non-overlapping channel assignments.
choices.explanation: Those are 5 GHz channels and cannot be used by a 2.4 GHz radio.

choices.text: Channels 1, 5, and 9, leaving channel 11 free for guest traffic on the same radio.
choices.explanation: Channels 1, 5, and 9 still overlap with each other in the 2.4 GHz band.

questions.tip: Recall the standard non-overlapping channel triple in the lowest Wi-Fi band.
questions.explanation:
The 2.4 GHz band only has three 20 MHz channels that do not overlap.

**Why it works:** Channels 1, 6, and 11 are spaced 25 MHz apart, so their 20 MHz channel widths fit side by side with no overlap.

**Why the others don't work:**
- 2, 7, 12: spacing of five overlaps; channel 12 is also restricted in some regions.
- 36, 40, 44: 5 GHz channels.
- 1, 5, 9: overlap with each other.

skills: 2.2: Explain wireless networking technologies.
questions.question:
A retailer is rolling out contactless payment terminals at the front counter. Customers tap a card or phone within a few centimetres of the reader to pay, and the data exchange must be very short range so passers-by cannot trigger transactions inadvertently.

Which wireless technology fits this contactless payment use case?

choices.text: NFC, which operates over a few centimetres and is designed for contactless payments and pairing taps.
choices.explanation: NFC's intentionally short range matches the tap-to-pay requirement.

choices.text: Bluetooth Low Energy, broadcasting a payment beacon up to 10 metres from the counter.
choices.explanation: Bluetooth ranges of several metres are far too long for a tap-to-pay model.

choices.text: Passive UHF RFID, allowing the terminal to read tags from across the shop floor.
choices.explanation: Passive UHF RFID is designed for multi-metre reads, opposite to the short-range requirement.

choices.text: Wi-Fi Direct, pairing the card and reader as a peer-to-peer wireless LAN session.
choices.explanation: Wi-Fi Direct has metres of range and is not how payment cards transact.

questions.tip: Focus on the wireless standard built specifically for centimetre-scale interactions.
questions.explanation:
Contactless payments rely on a wireless technology whose physical reach is only a few centimetres by design.

**Why it works:** NFC operates at 13.56 MHz and has an intentional reach of a few centimetres, which keeps inadvertent transactions out of scope.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Bluetooth LE: metres of range.
- UHF RFID: designed for multi-metre reads, e.g. inventory.
- Wi-Fi Direct: metres of range and a different protocol model.

skills: 2.2: Explain wireless networking technologies.
questions.question:
The IT manager has approved a refresh of the office wireless and wants to take advantage of the newly available spectrum that is exclusive to the latest Wi-Fi generation. The current APs only support 2.4 and 5 GHz, and the new APs must allow client devices in the additional spectrum to associate on dedicated channels.

Which 802.11 standard is required to use the 6 GHz band?

choices.text: 802.11ax operating in 6 GHz, marketed as Wi-Fi 6E for the extended band.
choices.explanation: Wi-Fi 6E is 802.11ax certified for operation in the new 6 GHz spectrum.

choices.text: 802.11ac, which originally introduced the 6 GHz band alongside 5 GHz operation.
choices.explanation: 802.11ac is a 5 GHz-only standard and cannot use the 6 GHz band.

choices.text: 802.11n, since dual-band radios were first defined in this standard and extended to 6 GHz.
choices.explanation: 802.11n supports 2.4 and 5 GHz only.

choices.text: 802.11g, with high-throughput channels added by an amendment for the 6 GHz spectrum.
choices.explanation: 802.11g is a legacy 2.4 GHz standard and has no 6 GHz capability.

questions.tip: Identify the Wi-Fi generation that first certified operation in the newest band.
questions.explanation:
The 6 GHz band was opened to Wi-Fi alongside the most recent generation of the 802.11 standard.

**Why it works:** 802.11ax devices certified as Wi-Fi 6E are explicitly authorised to operate on 6 GHz channels.

**Why the others don't work:**
- 802.11ac: 5 GHz only.
- 802.11n: 2.4 and 5 GHz only.
- 802.11g: 2.4 GHz only and legacy.

skills: 2.2: Explain wireless networking technologies.
questions.question:
A warehouse operations team wants to track palettes as they move through loading docks. The tags must be inexpensive enough to attach to every palette, must not require batteries, and need to be readable at distances of several metres as forklifts drive past portal readers.

Which TWO characteristics of the tracking technology are required to satisfy these constraints?

choices.text: Use passive tags that draw operating power from the reader's RF field rather than an onboard battery.
choices.explanation: Passive RFID tags are inexpensive and have no battery to maintain or replace.

choices.text: Operate in the UHF RFID band to support multi-metre reads of tags as they pass the portal.
choices.explanation: UHF RFID provides the read distance needed for vehicle-mounted scanning.

choices.text: Use NFC tags so each palette can be touched briefly by the dock worker on the way through.
choices.explanation: NFC requires centimetre-scale proximity and would not work for a portal read at distance.

choices.text: Deploy active battery-powered tags so each palette can broadcast its position continuously.
choices.explanation: Active tags conflict with the no-battery and low-cost constraints.

choices.text: Switch to Bluetooth Classic beacons paired one-by-one to a handheld scanner.
choices.explanation: Bluetooth pairing does not match the high-volume, drive-through read profile.

questions.tip: Look for the technology family that supports battery-free tags read at modest distance.
questions.explanation:
Industrial tracking that needs cheap tags and metres of read range maps to a specific RFID profile.

**Why it works:** Passive UHF RFID tags meet both constraints: they have no battery and they support multi-metre reads suitable for portal scanning.

**Why the others don't work:**
- NFC: too short range for drive-through reads.
- Active tags: have batteries, raising cost and maintenance.
- Bluetooth Classic: not suited to bulk drive-by scanning.

questions.question: Match each 802.11 standard to the band or bands it operates in.

choices.text: 2.4 GHz only
choices.explanation: 802.11g operates only in the 2.4 GHz band with rates up to 54 Mbps.

choices.text: 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz
choices.explanation: 802.11n introduced dual-band operation and MIMO.

choices.text: 5 GHz only
choices.explanation: 802.11ac operates exclusively in the 5 GHz band.

choices.text: 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz
choices.explanation: 802.11ax certified as Wi-Fi 6E adds 6 GHz on top of the existing two bands.

questions.tip: Map each standard to the bands its radios are certified to use.
questions.explanation: Each 802.11 generation operates in a defined set of bands, and recognising those bands is foundational to wireless troubleshooting and procurement.

skills: 2.3: Summarize services provided by networked hosts.
questions.question:
During an audit, the operations team is reviewing how Kerberos tickets are issued in the domain. The lead engineer points out that the cluster of replicated servers also handles account lockouts and certificate distribution to clients. The auditor asks the technician to identify the role these servers are fulfilling.

Which server role best describes a host that issues Kerberos tickets and enforces account lockout policies?

choices.text: An AAA server that authenticates users and authorises access to domain resources.
choices.explanation: AAA servers cover authentication, authorisation, and accounting, including Kerberos-based logon services.

choices.text: A syslog server that receives login event records from all domain controllers.
choices.explanation: Syslog servers collect log data and do not themselves issue authentication tickets.

choices.text: A fileshare server that controls per-folder permissions across the organisation.
choices.explanation: Fileshare servers serve files; permissions on the share rely on authentication done elsewhere.

choices.text: A print server that authenticates each print job before despatching it to the device.
choices.explanation: Print servers queue print jobs and rely on a separate authentication service.

questions.tip: Focus on the role responsible for authentication decisions in a domain.
questions.explanation:
The function of issuing tickets and enforcing logon policy maps to a specific server role.

**Why it works:** Authentication, authorisation, and accounting are the three functions of an AAA server, of which Kerberos-based logon is one common example.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Syslog: receives logs, does not authenticate.
- Fileshare: serves files only.
- Print: queues print jobs only.

skills: 2.3: Summarize services provided by networked hosts.
questions.question:
The marketing site has begun struggling under a product-launch traffic spike, and the operations team has provisioned three identical web hosts behind a single virtual IP address. They need an appliance that distributes incoming HTTPS sessions evenly across the back-end servers and stops sending requests to a host that fails its health probe.

Which internet appliance fits this requirement?

choices.text: A load balancer that distributes inbound connections across the pool and removes failed members from rotation.
choices.explanation: Load balancers split traffic across a pool and perform health checks to detect unhealthy backends.

choices.text: A proxy server that caches static assets on behalf of clients accessing the site.
choices.explanation: Caching proxies offload repeat requests but do not distribute across multiple backends.

choices.text: A spam gateway that filters inbound traffic for unwanted bulk messages.
choices.explanation: Spam gateways operate on mail flow, not web traffic distribution.

choices.text: A UTM appliance that bundles firewall, IDS, and antivirus into one device.
choices.explanation: UTM consolidates security functions but is not designed to distribute sessions across servers.

questions.tip: Focus on the appliance whose primary job is spreading traffic across a pool of hosts.
questions.explanation:
Spreading inbound sessions across a backend pool with health monitoring is a single, well-defined appliance role.

**Why it works:** Load balancers present a single virtual address to clients and forward traffic to healthy members of the backend pool.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Proxy: caches or forwards outbound traffic.
- Spam gateway: filters mail.
- UTM: bundles security functions, not load distribution.

skills: 2.3: Summarize services provided by networked hosts.
questions.question:
The security team has flagged that the firewall, IDS, antivirus gateway, and web filter at a branch site are running as four separate appliances, each consuming rack space and a separate maintenance contract. Management wants to collapse those functions into a single device while keeping the same protections.

Which appliance type should the team specify when sourcing the replacement?

choices.text: A UTM appliance that bundles firewall, IDS, antivirus, and content filtering into a single device.
choices.explanation: Unified threat management is purpose-built to consolidate multiple security functions on one platform.

choices.text: A reverse proxy that sits between clients and the internal web servers for SSL inspection.
choices.explanation: Reverse proxies handle inbound web traffic patterns and do not consolidate firewall and antivirus.

choices.text: A SCADA gateway that consolidates industrial control protocols for the site.
choices.explanation: SCADA gateways are industrial control devices, not enterprise security consolidators.

choices.text: A spam gateway that combines mail filtering with antivirus scanning.
choices.explanation: Spam gateways operate only on mail traffic, not on the full perimeter.

questions.tip: Find the appliance class defined by combining multiple security functions in one box.
questions.explanation:
Combining firewall, IDS, antivirus, and web filtering into one platform is the defining feature of one specific appliance class.

**Why it works:** A UTM device packages those security functions together so that one box and one console replace several discrete appliances.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Reverse proxy: web-traffic-specific.
- SCADA gateway: industrial control role.
- Spam gateway: mail-only.

skills: 2.3: Summarize services provided by networked hosts.
questions.question:
Security analysts at a manufacturing plant are reviewing the architecture used to monitor and control the assembly line. PLCs on the floor report sensor readings to a central host that operators interact with through HMI workstations, and the central host can issue commands back to the field devices.

Which category of system is being described?

choices.text: A SCADA system that supervises and controls industrial processes through PLCs and HMI consoles.
choices.explanation: SCADA platforms supervise field devices and present operator HMIs to monitor and control processes.

choices.text: A UTM appliance correlating field sensor data for security analysis.
choices.explanation: UTM is a security appliance, not an industrial control supervisor.

choices.text: An AAA server brokering access between assembly line workers and the HMI consoles.
choices.explanation: AAA handles authentication; it does not supervise PLCs or process data.

choices.text: A consumer IoT hub aggregating telemetry from smart appliances on the line.
choices.explanation: Consumer IoT hubs target home devices, not industrial PLCs and HMIs.

questions.tip: Match the description of HMI plus PLC plus central supervisor to the right system family.
questions.explanation:
PLC field devices, HMI operator consoles, and a central supervisor together define a specific class of legacy/embedded system.

**Why it works:** SCADA is the standard label for industrial supervisory control systems built around HMIs and PLCs.

**Why the others don't work:**
- UTM: a security appliance.
- AAA: an authentication service.
- Consumer IoT hub: a different class of device entirely.

skills: 2.3: Summarize services provided by networked hosts.
questions.question:
A new branch office is being commissioned and the network engineer is finalising which server roles to deploy on the local appliance. Each workstation must obtain its IP automatically on boot, and the centralised security operations centre wants every authentication event from the branch forwarded to a central log collector.

Which TWO server roles directly satisfy these requirements?

choices.text: Deploy a DHCP server to lease IP addresses to workstations on boot.
choices.explanation: DHCP automates IP configuration for clients joining the LAN.

choices.text: Forward authentication and system events to a syslog server at the SOC for centralised retention.
choices.explanation: Syslog is the standard mechanism for centralising event logs from multiple hosts.

choices.text: Stand up a NTP server so workstations request DHCP leases at consistent intervals.
choices.explanation: NTP synchronises time and is not what triggers DHCP leases.

choices.text: Stand up a print server to relay authentication tokens to the SOC over a job channel.
choices.explanation: Print servers handle print jobs, not authentication logging.

choices.text: Stand up a database server to issue dynamic IPs from a record store.
choices.explanation: Database servers store application data; they are not the IP lease service.

questions.tip: Pair each requirement with the role whose primary purpose is exactly that function.
questions.explanation:
Automatic IP addressing and centralised event logging map cleanly to two well-defined server roles.

**Why it works:** DHCP issues leases on boot, and syslog collects events from many hosts for retention and analysis.

**Why the others don't work:**
- NTP: time synchronisation, not IP issuance.
- Print server: print queue role.
- Database server: structured data storage, not IP leasing.

skills: 2.3: Summarize services provided by networked hosts.
questions.question: Match each internet-facing appliance to its primary role.

choices.text: Filters inbound mail for unsolicited bulk messages and known malware payloads
choices.explanation: Spam gateways inspect SMTP traffic for nuisance and malicious mail.

choices.text: Distributes incoming sessions across a pool of backend servers with health checking
choices.explanation: Load balancers spread traffic across a pool and remove unhealthy members.

choices.text: Sits between clients and the wider internet to mediate, cache, or filter outbound requests
choices.explanation: Proxy servers mediate outbound client requests for performance and policy enforcement.

choices.text: Combines firewall, IDS, antivirus, and web filtering on a single perimeter device
choices.explanation: UTM appliances consolidate multiple security functions in one platform.

questions.tip: Map each appliance to the single role that best defines its purpose at the perimeter.
questions.explanation: Each internet appliance has a distinct primary purpose, and the categories rarely overlap even when vendors bundle them.

skills: 2.4: Explain common network configuration concepts.
questions.question:
The mail administrator at a charity has been told their newsletters keep landing in recipients' junk folders. After confirming the mail server is reputable, the administrator wants to publish a DNS record listing the IP addresses authorised to send mail on behalf of the domain so recipients can verify the source.

Which DNS record type should the administrator publish?

choices.text: A `TXT` record containing the `SPF` policy that lists authorised sending IPs for the domain.
choices.explanation: `SPF` is published as a `TXT` record naming the IPs allowed to send mail for the domain.

choices.text: An `MX` record pointing to the IPs allowed to send mail on behalf of the domain.
choices.explanation: `MX` records direct inbound mail to mailbox hosts; they do not authorise senders.

choices.text: A `CNAME` record aliasing the sending hosts to the corporate domain.
choices.explanation: `CNAME` provides name aliases and does not communicate sender authorisation.

choices.text: An `AAAA` record pointing to the IPv6 address of the outbound mail relay.
choices.explanation: `AAAA` records resolve a name to an IPv6 address; they do not list authorised senders.

questions.tip: Look for the record family used to publish text-based mail authorisation policies.
questions.explanation:
Authorised sender lists for a domain are published in a specific DNS record format.

**Why it works:** `SPF` policies live in `TXT` records and enumerate the IP addresses that are permitted to send mail using the domain.

**Why the others don't work:**
- MX: routes inbound mail to mailbox hosts.
- `CNAME`: name alias.
- `AAAA`: IPv6 host record.

skills: 2.4: Explain common network configuration concepts.
questions.question:
A network engineer has been asked to keep a department's networked label printer at the same IPv4 address even though it boots from DHCP. The printer must continue to receive its lease automatically, and the engineer wants to avoid configuring a static address on the device itself.

Which DHCP feature should the engineer use?

choices.text: A DHCP reservation that ties the printer's MAC address to a specific IP within the scope.
choices.explanation: Reservations bind a MAC to a fixed lease while keeping DHCP in charge of configuration.

choices.text: A DHCP exclusion for the printer's IP so the lease never expires.
choices.explanation: Exclusions remove addresses from the pool entirely, they do not assign them to a device.

choices.text: A second DHCP scope that contains only the printer's IP address.
choices.explanation: A scope defines a range; a second scope for a single device is not how addressing is fixed.

choices.text: An infinite lease duration on the existing scope so all clients keep their addresses.
choices.explanation: Infinite leases apply to every client and do not guarantee the printer keeps the same IP after a long outage.

questions.tip: Look for the DHCP feature that binds a MAC address to a fixed IP within the scope.
questions.explanation:
Keeping a DHCP client on the same address without configuring it manually is a defined DHCP feature.

**Why it works:** A reservation associates the device's MAC address with a chosen IP inside the scope, so the DHCP server hands out the same lease every time.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Exclusion: removes the address from being leased to anyone.
- Extra scope: scopes define ranges, not single-device pinning.
- Infinite lease: applies broadly and is not a per-device guarantee.

skills: 2.4: Explain common network configuration concepts.
questions.question:
An office has one physical switch connecting workstations, voice phones, and a guest Wi-Fi access point. Management wants the three groups isolated at layer 2 even though they share the same switch hardware, so a broadcast on the guest network never reaches the corporate desktops.

Which network configuration achieves this isolation?

choices.text: Assign each group of ports to its own VLAN so broadcast domains are separated logically on the switch.
choices.explanation: VLANs create separate layer 2 broadcast domains on the same physical switch.

choices.text: Configure a VPN between the guest network and the corporate network for traffic separation.
choices.explanation: VPNs tunnel traffic across untrusted networks; they do not isolate ports on a switch.

choices.text: Set up separate DHCP scopes for each group while leaving all ports in the same broadcast domain.
choices.explanation: Separate scopes do not stop broadcast traffic from being shared across the same VLAN.

choices.text: Enable DNS suffix search lists per port so each group sees only its own services.
choices.explanation: DNS suffixes affect name resolution and do not isolate layer 2 broadcast traffic.

questions.tip: Find the layer 2 technology designed to split a single switch into multiple broadcast domains.
questions.explanation:
Splitting groups of switch ports so their broadcasts stay separate is exactly the purpose of one layer 2 technology.

**Why it works:** VLANs assign port groups to independent broadcast domains, so guest traffic and corporate traffic are isolated even though they share the switch.

**Why the others don't work:**
- VPN: an overlay tunnel, not a port-isolation mechanism.
- Multiple DHCP scopes: do not change layer 2 boundaries.
- DNS suffix lists: affect resolution, not switching.

skills: 2.4: Explain common network configuration concepts.
questions.question:
Following a move to home working, the IT manager wants remote staff to access internal file shares as if they were in the office. The solution must encrypt all traffic across the public internet and present each remote machine with an internal corporate IP address from the office subnet.

Which technology fits these requirements?

choices.text: A remote-access VPN that encrypts traffic and assigns each client an IP inside the corporate network.
choices.explanation: Remote-access VPNs encapsulate and encrypt the tunnel and place the client logically inside the LAN.

choices.text: A VLAN extension that stretches the corporate broadcast domain to each home worker over the internet.
choices.explanation: VLANs operate within a switched LAN and are not how remote workers tunnel across the internet.

choices.text: An additional DHCP scope sized to lease addresses directly to remote workers' home routers.
choices.explanation: DHCP does not encrypt traffic or extend a corporate subnet over the internet.

choices.text: DNS forwarders that redirect each remote worker's traffic via internal name resolution.
choices.explanation: DNS forwarders direct name lookups; they do not move user traffic onto the corporate LAN.

questions.tip: Look for the technology that combines encryption with logical placement inside the LAN.
questions.explanation:
Encrypting remote traffic across the internet and placing the client inside the corporate IP range is the textbook role of one specific technology.

**Why it works:** A remote-access VPN tunnels the user's traffic over an encrypted channel and assigns them an address inside the corporate network.

**Why the others don't work:**
- VLAN: a LAN-only technology.
- DHCP scope: does not encrypt or extend the LAN over the internet.
- DNS forwarder: name resolution only.

skills: 2.4: Explain common network configuration concepts.
questions.question:
After repeated reports of phishing pretending to be from the company, the IT lead is putting in place additional mail authentication. They have already published `SPF`, and they want recipients to be able to verify that messages are cryptographically signed by the domain and to receive instructions about what to do with messages that fail those checks.

Which TWO additional records should be published?

choices.text: A `DKIM` record exposing the public key recipients use to verify the signature on each message.
choices.explanation: `DKIM` publishes the verification key so receivers can confirm message signatures.

choices.text: A `DMARC` record telling receivers what policy to apply when `SPF` or `DKIM` checks fail.
choices.explanation: `DMARC` ties `SPF` and `DKIM` together and specifies the disposition for failing mail.

choices.text: An additional `MX` record for the outbound relay so signed messages are routed correctly.
choices.explanation: `MX` records concern inbound delivery and do not influence signing or policy.

choices.text: A `CNAME` alias from the apex domain to the cryptographic signer's hostname.
choices.explanation: `CNAME` aliases at the apex are not how `DKIM` keys or `DMARC` policies are published.

choices.text: A second `SPF` `TXT` record adding more authorised senders to broaden coverage.
choices.explanation: Multiple `SPF` records cause `SPF` to fail; only one `SPF` record should exist per domain.

questions.tip: Identify which records publish signing keys and policy guidance for receivers.
questions.explanation:
Combining cryptographic signatures with policy enforcement maps to two specific mail authentication records.

**Why it works:** `DKIM` publishes the verification key for signed messages, and `DMARC` tells receivers how to handle messages that fail `SPF` or `DKIM` checks.

**Why the others don't work:**
- MX: routes inbound mail.
- `CNAME` at apex: not how `DKIM` or `DMARC` are deployed.
- Second `SPF` record: breaks `SPF` rather than extending it.

skills: 2.4: Explain common network configuration concepts.
questions.question: Match each DNS record type to the value it returns or publishes.

choices.text: Maps a hostname to an IPv4 address
choices.explanation: A records carry IPv4 host addresses.

choices.text: Maps a hostname to an IPv6 address
choices.explanation: `AAAA` records carry IPv6 host addresses.

choices.text: Aliases one hostname to another canonical hostname
choices.explanation: `CNAME` records point to another name to be resolved further.

choices.text: Identifies the mail server responsible for accepting mail for the domain
choices.explanation: `MX` records direct inbound mail to mailbox hosts in priority order.

questions.tip: Match each record type to the resource it returns at resolution time.
questions.explanation: Each DNS record type returns a defined value and recognising those mappings is fundamental to troubleshooting name resolution.

skills: 2.5: Compare and contrast common networking hardware devices.
questions.question:
During a fibre-to-the-premises installation, the technician traces the incoming cable from the street and finds a small wall-mounted device with a fibre input and a copper Ethernet output that feeds the customer's router. The installer tells the homeowner that this device converts the optical signal into Ethernet for the building.

Which device is being described?

choices.text: An ONT, which terminates the fibre service and presents an Ethernet handoff to the customer.
choices.explanation: Optical network terminals convert the incoming fibre signal to Ethernet at the customer premises.

choices.text: A cable modem, which converts the coax broadband signal to Ethernet for the home network.
choices.explanation: Cable modems handle coax DOCSIS, not fibre.

choices.text: A DSL modem, which terminates the copper telephone line as Ethernet for the home network.
choices.explanation: DSL modems terminate copper telephone lines, not fibre.

choices.text: A managed switch, providing fibre uplink and copper downlink ports for the customer.
choices.explanation: Switches forward Ethernet between ports; they are not the fibre service termination.

questions.tip: Look for the device whose only job is to terminate the fibre service at the premises.
questions.explanation:
The customer-side endpoint of a fibre service is a specific named device.

**Why it works:** An ONT terminates the optical signal and presents an Ethernet handoff that the customer's router plugs into.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Cable modem: coax broadband, not fibre.
- DSL modem: copper phone line, not fibre.
- Managed switch: forwards Ethernet, does not terminate the service.

skills: 2.5: Compare and contrast common networking hardware devices.
questions.question:
An office is deploying a single ceiling-mounted wireless access point in a meeting room. There is no power outlet near the ceiling, but a single Ethernet cable already runs from the comms cupboard to the mounting point, and the existing switch is a basic unmanaged unit with no PoE capability.

Which device should the technician fit so the AP receives both data and power down that one cable?

choices.text: A PoE injector inserted in line between the unmanaged switch and the AP's cable run.
choices.explanation: Injectors add PoE to a single link without requiring a PoE-capable switch.

choices.text: A second unmanaged switch at the AP end of the cable to split data and power.
choices.explanation: A switch does not add PoE; it just forwards Ethernet.

choices.text: A patch panel between the switch and the AP to provide PoE termination.
choices.explanation: Patch panels are passive terminations and do not supply power.

choices.text: A network tap inserted in line to provide an out-of-band power feed.
choices.explanation: Network taps duplicate traffic for monitoring; they do not supply power.

questions.tip: Find the device that adds PoE to a single link without replacing the switch.
questions.explanation:
Adding PoE on a single link without changing the switch is solved by a specific in-line device.

**Why it works:** A PoE injector adds the DC voltage to the Ethernet pairs between the unmanaged switch and the AP, delivering both power and data over the existing cable.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Second unmanaged switch: does not generate PoE.
- Patch panel: passive termination only.
- Network tap: a monitoring device, not a power source.

skills: 2.5: Compare and contrast common networking hardware devices.
questions.question:
Cabling for a refurbished office has been pulled to the comms cupboard, and the installer needs to terminate the wall socket runs so they can be patched to the switch with short pre-made leads. The chosen device must allow each fixed run to be terminated once and then patched flexibly without re-terminating the structured cable.

Which device should be installed in the cupboard?

choices.text: A patch panel that punches down the fixed runs at the back and presents RJ45 sockets for short patch leads at the front.
choices.explanation: Patch panels separate permanent cable terminations from flexible patching to active equipment.

choices.text: An unmanaged switch onto which each fixed run is punched down for direct patching.
choices.explanation: Switches do not provide a punch-down termination surface for structured cabling.

choices.text: A firewall providing the structured termination point between the workstations and the LAN.
choices.explanation: Firewalls enforce policy at boundaries; they are not cable termination devices.

choices.text: A cable modem to consolidate the fixed runs into the WAN uplink.
choices.explanation: Cable modems terminate the broadband service, not the LAN's internal cabling.

questions.tip: Identify the passive termination point used between fixed cable runs and active equipment.
questions.explanation:
Fixed structured cabling and active switch ports are linked by a specific passive device.

**Why it works:** A patch panel punches down the fixed runs at the rear and presents RJ45 sockets at the front so short patch leads connect them to the switch.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Unmanaged switch: an active forwarding device.
- Firewall: a policy-enforcement device.
- Cable modem: a service termination, not a structured-cable termination.

skills: 2.5: Compare and contrast common networking hardware devices.
questions.question:
The operations team is reviewing addresses learned on the access switches. The senior engineer reminds a new starter that the burned-in 48-bit identifier each NIC presents on the wire is unique to that adapter and is what the switch uses to populate its forwarding table.

Which term refers to this 48-bit hardware identifier on the NIC?

choices.text: The MAC address, a 48-bit identifier burned into the NIC and used by the switch's forwarding table.
choices.explanation: MAC addresses are the layer 2 identifiers switches use to forward frames.

choices.text: The IPv4 address assigned to the NIC by the DHCP server on boot.
choices.explanation: IPv4 addresses operate at layer 3 and are leased rather than burned in.
