- 600 W: zero headroom.

skills: 3.6: Given a scenario, install the appropriate power supply.
questions.question:
Routing cables in a small chassis with limited airflow is a priority for a new build. The technician wants to install only the power cables the system actually needs, leaving unused leads outside the case to improve airflow and cleanliness.

Which PSU feature supports this requirement?

choices.text: Modular PSU with detachable cables for unused rails.
choices.explanation: Modular PSUs let the builder omit unused cables.

choices.text: Redundant PSU with two interchangeable units sharing the load.
choices.explanation: Redundancy addresses uptime, not cable count.

choices.text: Higher wattage non-modular PSU for additional headroom.
choices.explanation: Non-modular units include all cables permanently attached.

choices.text: Active PFC PSU for cleaner mains current draw.
choices.explanation: PFC affects input current quality, not cable management.

questions.tip: Identify the PSU design that allows cables to be attached only as needed.
questions.explanation:
A modular PSU has detachable cables on the PSU side, so the builder connects only what is required.

**Why it works:** Unused cables stay out of the case, improving airflow and aesthetics.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Redundant: uptime feature.
- Higher wattage non-modular: still has all cables attached.
- PFC: input characteristic.

skills: 3.6: Given a scenario, install the appropriate power supply.
questions.question:
While installing a power supply in a modern desktop, the technician notes that the 24-pin motherboard connector arrives as a 20-pin connector with a detachable 4-pin segment. The motherboard exposes a full 24-pin header.

How should the technician connect the motherboard power?

choices.text: Attach the 4-pin segment to the 20-pin connector to form a single 24-pin connector.
choices.explanation: The 20+4 design exists to fit either 20-pin or 24-pin headers.

choices.text: Leave the 4-pin segment unconnected since modern boards do not need it.
choices.explanation: Modern boards need the full 24 pins for proper rail delivery.

choices.text: Use only the 4-pin segment because the board already has standby power.
choices.explanation: Standby power does not replace the main 24-pin connector.

choices.text: Connect the 4-pin segment to the CPU EPS header instead.
choices.explanation: CPU EPS uses a different keyed connector.

questions.tip: The 20+4 design is meant to combine for full-size headers.
questions.explanation:
The 20+4 pin motherboard connector clips together to provide the 24-pin power required by modern boards.

**Why it works:** The two segments key together and slot into the 24-pin header as one connector.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Leaving 4-pin off: starves the board.
- 4-pin alone: insufficient.
- CPU EPS: wrong header and keying.

skills: 3.6: Given a scenario, install the appropriate power supply.
questions.question:
A small business is specifying PSUs for a new rack of file servers. Uptime is critical because file shares serve the entire office, and the team wants the systems to remain online if one PSU fails or a single circuit drops.

Which TWO PSU features should be specified?

choices.text: Redundant power supplies with two hot-swappable units per server.
choices.explanation: Redundant PSUs allow continued operation through a single PSU failure.

choices.text: Each PSU fed from a separate circuit so a single-circuit drop does not affect both inputs.
choices.explanation: Dual feeds isolate against single-circuit outages.

choices.text: Lowest-cost non-modular PSU with no redundancy to save budget.
choices.explanation: Cost savings here defeat the uptime goal.

choices.text: Single PSU per server with a high efficiency rating.
choices.explanation: Efficiency does not provide redundancy on its own.

choices.text: Disable PSU fans to reduce mechanical wear and increase uptime.
choices.explanation: Disabling cooling causes overheating and failure.

questions.tip: Combine PSU redundancy with feed diversity at the circuit level.
questions.explanation:
Hot-swappable redundant PSUs combined with two distinct mains feeds protect against both PSU and circuit-level failures.

**Why it works:** Failure of any single PSU or circuit leaves the server running on the other path.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Cheapest non-modular: defeats redundancy.
- Single PSU with efficiency: no redundancy.
- Disable fans: causes failure.

skills: 3.6: Given a scenario, install the appropriate power supply.
questions.question: Match each PSU output rail to the components it primarily powers.

choices.text: Supplies low-voltage logic and memory subsystems on the motherboard
choices.explanation: +3.3V feeds chipset and memory rails.

choices.text: Powers older logic chips and some USB and SATA logic on the motherboard
choices.explanation: +5V is the legacy logic rail still used in modern boards.

choices.text: Drives CPUs, GPUs, fans, and mechanical drive motors, carrying most modern system power
choices.explanation: +12V handles the heavy loads of CPUs, GPUs, and motors.

choices.text: The primary motherboard connector that delivers all main rails to the board's regulators
choices.explanation: The 20+4 connector carries 3.3V, 5V, 12V, and standby pins to the board.

questions.tip: Match each voltage to the component class it serves.
questions.explanation: Modern PSUs route 3.3V and 5V to logic, 12V to heavy loads, and feed all rails to the board through the 20+4 pin main connector.

skills: 3.7: Given a scenario, deploy and configure multifunction devices/printers and settings.
questions.question:
During the rollout of a new multifunction printer to an open-plan office, the technician unboxes the device and prepares to install it. The office layout has the only Ethernet drop near a window, but staff would prefer the printer next to the photocopy area further from the drop.

What should the technician consider FIRST when choosing the printer's final location?

choices.text: Network and power availability at the proposed location, plus ventilation and access for users.
choices.explanation: Setup planning addresses connectivity, power, ventilation, and physical access.

choices.text: Whether the device firmware can be downgraded for older drivers.
choices.explanation: Firmware version is unrelated to physical setup location.

choices.text: Whether to enable secured print release before configuring drivers.
choices.explanation: Secure print is a downstream config step, not a location decision.

choices.text: Which PCL or PostScript driver to install on the print server.
choices.explanation: Driver choice happens after the device is sited and on the network.

questions.tip: Setup begins with picking a viable physical and network location.
questions.explanation:
Site planning is the first deployment task: power, network, and physical layout determine where the device can actually function.

**Why it works:** Without network, power, and clearance, no software step will help.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Firmware downgrade: not part of siting.
- Secured prints: later configuration step.
- Driver choice: comes after physical install.

skills: 3.7: Given a scenario, deploy and configure multifunction devices/printers and settings.
questions.question:
A design studio relies on Adobe applications that output complex vector artwork directly to the office printer. The artwork includes Type 1 fonts and PDF transparency that must render without rasterising on the workstation.

Which print driver language should the technician install?

choices.text: PostScript driver to faithfully render Adobe vector artwork on the device.
choices.explanation: PostScript is the native language of Adobe's professional output pipeline.

choices.text: PCL driver because it processes vector data faster on shared printers.
choices.explanation: PCL renders some vector elements but is not the studio standard for Adobe output.

choices.text: Generic raster driver to standardise output across all clients.
choices.explanation: Rasterising defeats the requirement to preserve vector quality.

choices.text: Manufacturer print monitor only, with no page description language.
choices.explanation: A print monitor alone cannot interpret PostScript content.

questions.tip: Match the driver language to Adobe's preferred print pipeline.
questions.explanation:
PostScript is the page description language used by Adobe applications and produces accurate vector output.

**Why it works:** The printer's PostScript interpreter handles fonts and transparency natively.

**Why the others don't work:**
- PCL: less faithful for complex Adobe vector content.
- Raster: loses vector fidelity.
- Monitor only: no rendering capability.

skills: 3.7: Given a scenario, deploy and configure multifunction devices/printers and settings.
questions.question:
Staff in a shared workspace have complained that printed documents containing sensitive information are sometimes collected by the wrong person from the output tray. The MFP supports user authentication and badge readers, and the IT team wants to address the issue without restricting who can print.

Which configuration should the team enable?

choices.text: Secured print release that holds jobs at the device until the user authenticates locally.
choices.explanation: Secured print holds the job at the MFP until the owner authenticates.

choices.text: Disable network printing and require all jobs to come via USB drive.
choices.explanation: USB workflow blocks general printing and is impractical.

choices.text: Enable duplex printing to reduce the volume of paper in the tray.
choices.explanation: Duplex reduces paper but does not protect confidentiality.

choices.text: Configure the MFP to email users when their job has been printed.
choices.explanation: Email notifications do not prevent the wrong person collecting the page.

questions.tip: Look for the feature that holds output until the owner is at the device.
questions.explanation:
Secured (or pull) print holds jobs in a queue and releases them only after the user authenticates at the MFP.

**Why it works:** Pages do not print until the rightful owner is standing at the device.

**Why the others don't work:**
- USB only: blocks workflow.
- Duplex: unrelated to confidentiality.
- Email notifications: do not stop the wrong collector.

skills: 3.7: Given a scenario, deploy and configure multifunction devices/printers and settings.
questions.question:
The HR department needs to scan stacks of multi-page contracts to network folders for archival. The MFP supports several scan-to-destination options, and the team wants the scans to land in a shared Windows file share with controlled access.

Which network scan service should the technician configure?

choices.text: Scan to SMB share targeting the HR shared folder with credentials managed by the directory.
choices.explanation: SMB is the protocol for Windows file shares.

choices.text: Scan to email using each contract recipient's personal mailbox.
choices.explanation: Email is not a controlled archive destination for shared HR files.

choices.text: Scan to USB drive plugged into the MFP for each batch.
choices.explanation: USB workflow does not provide centralised access control.

choices.text: Scan to local hard disk on the MFP and rely on monthly export.
choices.explanation: Local MFP storage is not a long-term archive.

questions.tip: Match the scan destination to a Windows-controlled share protocol.
questions.explanation:
Scan-to-SMB writes scanned files directly to a Windows file share with directory-controlled permissions.

**Why it works:** Files land in the access-controlled HR share for archiving.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Email: not an archive control.
- USB: not centralised.
- Local MFP disk: not a managed share.

skills: 3.7: Given a scenario, deploy and configure multifunction devices/printers and settings.
questions.question:
The IT team is configuring a multifunction printer that will be shared by all departments. Management has asked for accountability over who prints what, and the device must integrate with the existing directory accounts so it does not maintain its own local user database.

Which TWO settings should be enabled?

choices.text: User authentication tied to the corporate directory, requiring sign-in before use.
choices.explanation: Directory-backed authentication ties usage to known accounts.

choices.text: Audit logging of print, copy, and scan activity per authenticated user.
choices.explanation: Audit logs provide accountability for usage.

choices.text: Anonymous walk-up printing for all jobs to simplify access.
choices.explanation: Anonymous use defeats accountability.

choices.text: Disable network discovery so the printer is hidden from clients.
choices.explanation: Hiding the printer prevents users from printing at all.

choices.text: Default duplex on, monochrome only to reduce waste.
choices.explanation: Print mode defaults do not address accountability.

questions.tip: Combine identity binding with usage logging.
questions.explanation:
Directory-tied authentication and audit logging are the standard pair for printer accountability.

**Why it works:** Every job is attributable to a directory user and logged for review.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Anonymous: no identity.
- Hide printer: no usage.
- Duplex defaults: unrelated to accountability.

skills: 3.7: Given a scenario, deploy and configure multifunction devices/printers and settings.
questions.question: Match each printer deployment option to the description that best identifies it.

choices.text: A printer attached to one workstation and shared on the network through that machine
choices.explanation: Workstation-shared printers depend on the host PC being on.

choices.text: A dedicated server that manages print queues, drivers, and access for many users
choices.explanation: Print servers centralise queue management and driver deployment.

choices.text: A mechanism that feeds a stack of pages through the scanner for batch capture
choices.explanation: ADFs handle batch scans without manual page changes.

choices.text: A glass platen where individual pages, books, or non-standard items are placed for scanning
choices.explanation: Flatbeds accommodate bound or oversized originals.

questions.tip: Distinguish workstation-shared printing, centralised servers, and scanner input methods.
questions.explanation: Each option serves a distinct deployment or scanning function within an MFP environment.

skills: 3.8: Given a scenario, perform appropriate printer maintenance.
questions.question:
Users in the accounts office report that prints from the workgroup laser printer have started showing faded text and streaks down the page. The device's onboard counter shows the printer has passed its rated page count for routine servicing.

Which maintenance task should the technician perform FIRST?

choices.text: Apply the manufacturer's maintenance kit, which includes fuser, rollers, and transfer components.
choices.explanation: A laser maintenance kit replaces wear parts at the rated interval and clears typical faded-print symptoms.

choices.text: Clean the printhead nozzles with the inkjet utility.
choices.explanation: Laser printers do not have inkjet printheads.

choices.text: Replace the ribbon and check the printhead pin alignment.
choices.explanation: Ribbons are impact-printer components, not laser.

choices.text: Clean the thermal heating element and reseat the paper roll.
choices.explanation: Heating elements and rolls are thermal printer parts.

questions.tip: Match the maintenance task to the laser technology in use.
questions.explanation:
Laser maintenance kits replace consumable wear parts (fuser, rollers, transfer) at scheduled intervals.

**Why it works:** Worn rollers and fuser cause the streaking and fading described.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Inkjet printhead: wrong technology.
- Ribbon: impact printer.
- Heating element: thermal printer.

skills: 3.8: Given a scenario, perform appropriate printer maintenance.
questions.question:
An office inkjet printer that has sat unused for several weeks now produces output with banding and missing colour bands across all test prints. Cartridges have plenty of ink remaining and were installed last month.

Which maintenance step should the technician perform?

choices.text: Run the printer's printhead cleaning utility to clear dried ink from the nozzles.
choices.explanation: Dried ink in nozzles is the typical cause after a long idle period.

choices.text: Replace the fuser unit and recalibrate registration.
choices.explanation: Fuser units are laser components, not inkjet.

choices.text: Replace the impact ribbon and inspect the printhead pins.
choices.explanation: Ribbons and pins are impact printer parts.

choices.text: Replace the thermal feed assembly and roll.
choices.explanation: Thermal components do not apply to inkjet.

questions.tip: Identify the inkjet-specific maintenance task that addresses dried ink.
questions.explanation:
Inkjet printhead cleaning utilities purge dried ink from the nozzle plate using the printer's built-in cleaning cycle.

**Why it works:** Banding from dried nozzles is reversed by repeated cleaning cycles.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Fuser: laser only.
- Ribbon: impact only.
- Thermal feed: thermal only.

skills: 3.8: Given a scenario, perform appropriate printer maintenance.
questions.question:
A retail checkout uses a thermal receipt printer that prints receipts directly without ink or ribbon. Cashiers report that recent receipts come out blank even though the paper feeds normally and the printer reports no error.

What is the MOST likely cause?

choices.text: The paper roll has been loaded with the wrong side facing the heating element, or non-thermal paper has been used.
choices.explanation: Thermal paper has a heat-sensitive coating on one side only.

choices.text: The toner cartridge has run dry and needs replacement.
choices.explanation: Thermal printers do not use toner.

choices.text: The inkjet printheads need a deep clean cycle.
choices.explanation: Thermal printers do not have inkjet heads.

choices.text: The ribbon has worn and needs replacement.
choices.explanation: Thermal printers do not use ribbons.

questions.tip: Recall that thermal printers rely on heat-sensitive paper.
questions.explanation:
Thermal printers darken treated paper using a heating element; loading the paper upside down or using untreated paper produces blank receipts.

**Why it works:** Only one face of thermal paper reacts to heat; the wrong orientation prints nothing.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Toner: laser only.
- Inkjet heads: wrong technology.
- Ribbon: impact only.

skills: 3.8: Given a scenario, perform appropriate printer maintenance.
questions.question:
A warehouse uses an impact printer to produce multipart shipping forms with carbonless copies. Operators report that the most recent prints are faint on the original page and nearly invisible on the back copies.

Which maintenance action will address the issue?

choices.text: Replace the worn ribbon so the printhead pins can transfer fresh ink through all copies.
choices.explanation: Impact printers rely on a ribbon; faded copies indicate it is exhausted.

choices.text: Run a deep clean on the inkjet printheads.
choices.explanation: Impact printers are not inkjets.

choices.text: Replace the laser toner cartridge and recalibrate.
choices.explanation: Impact printers do not use toner.

choices.text: Replace the thermal paper roll with a fresh batch.
choices.explanation: Multipart forms are not thermal.

questions.tip: Identify the consumable specific to impact printing.
questions.explanation:
Impact printers strike a ribbon against the paper; once the ribbon is exhausted prints fade.

**Why it works:** Replacing the ribbon restores ink transfer through all multipart layers.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Inkjet head clean: wrong tech.
- Toner: laser only.
- Thermal paper: wrong medium.

skills: 3.8: Given a scenario, perform appropriate printer maintenance.
questions.question:
A shared workgroup laser printer is showing combined symptoms across the department: print quality is faded, some pages show colour cast in graphics output, and a recent paper jam left small debris inside the paper path.

Which TWO maintenance actions should the technician perform?

choices.text: Replace the depleted toner cartridge and run a calibration cycle for colour alignment.
choices.explanation: Toner replacement and calibration address faded output and colour casts.

choices.text: Clean the interior paper path to remove debris left by the recent jam.
choices.explanation: Debris in the path causes future jams and quality issues.

choices.text: Replace the inkjet printheads and run a nozzle test pattern.
choices.explanation: Inkjet maintenance is not relevant to a laser printer.

choices.text: Replace the impact ribbon and inspect printhead pins.
choices.explanation: Impact parts are not present on a laser printer.

choices.text: Replace the thermal heating element and feed assembly.
choices.explanation: Thermal components are not relevant to a laser printer.

questions.tip: Combine consumable replacement and calibration with path cleaning.
questions.explanation:
Laser maintenance for the described symptoms includes replacing toner with calibration and cleaning the interior to remove jam debris.

**Why it works:** Calibration after toner replacement corrects colour registration; cleaning prevents repeat jams.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Inkjet, impact, thermal actions: wrong technology.

skills: 3.8: Given a scenario, perform appropriate printer maintenance.
questions.question: Match each printer technology to the appropriate maintenance task for that device.

choices.text: Replace toner, apply the maintenance kit, calibrate, and clean the paper path
choices.explanation: Standard laser maintenance set.

choices.text: Clean printheads, replace ink cartridges, calibrate, and clear jams in the carriage area
choices.explanation: Standard inkjet maintenance set.

choices.text: Replace the special heat-sensitive paper, clean the heating element, and remove debris from the feed assembly
choices.explanation: Standard thermal maintenance set.

choices.text: Replace the ribbon, replace the printhead pins when worn, and load multipart paper correctly
choices.explanation: Standard impact maintenance set.

questions.tip: Match each technology to its specific consumables and cleaning steps.
questions.explanation: Each printer technology has a distinct set of consumables and cleaning routines; mixing them risks damage or no improvement.

skills: 4.1: Explain virtualization concepts.
questions.question:
A developer needs to test a piece of malware safely without risking the host operating system or any other systems on the corporate network. The lab workstation runs Windows 11, and the malware sample must be detonated and observed in an isolated environment that can be reverted to a clean state afterwards.

Which use of a virtual machine BEST describes this scenario?

choices.text: A sandbox VM used to safely execute and analyse untrusted code in isolation from the host.
choices.explanation: Sandboxing is the canonical VM use case for malware analysis and untrusted code execution.

choices.text: A cross-platform virtualization VM used to run macOS applications on a Windows host.
choices.explanation: Cross-platform virtualization is about running a different guest OS family, not isolating malware.

choices.text: A VDI session brokered from a central server so the developer can roam between thin clients.
choices.explanation: VDI delivers centrally hosted desktops to end users, it is not focused on malware isolation.

choices.text: An application virtualization wrapper that streams legacy software to the developer's desktop.
choices.explanation: Application virtualization packages legacy apps for delivery, it does not isolate the host from malicious behaviour.

questions.tip: Consider which VM purpose specifically targets isolating untrusted or potentially harmful code.
questions.explanation:
A sandbox virtual machine provides a contained, disposable environment for detonating malware.

**Why it works:** The VM isolates the malicious binary from the host kernel and the physical network, and snapshots allow the analyst to revert to a known good state after each run.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Cross-platform virtualization: addresses running a different guest OS, not safety from malicious code.
- VDI: is a desktop delivery model, not a malware analysis pattern.
- Application virtualization: packages and streams applications, it does not provide a malware containment boundary.

skills: 4.1: Explain virtualization concepts.
questions.question:
The infrastructure team is consolidating ten physical servers onto a single new host. They want the hypervisor to run directly on the server hardware with no general purpose operating system underneath, to maximise performance and reduce the attack surface.

Which type of hypervisor meets this requirement?

choices.text: A Type 1 hypervisor installed bare metal on the server, such as VMware ESXi.
choices.explanation: Type 1 hypervisors run directly on hardware with no host OS in between.

choices.text: A Type 2 hypervisor installed on top of Windows Server, such as VMware Workstation.
choices.explanation: Type 2 hypervisors require a host operating system, which adds overhead and attack surface.

choices.text: A container runtime such as Docker installed on a Linux host.
choices.explanation: Containers share the host kernel and are not hypervisors at all.

choices.text: A VDI connection broker that streams desktops from a central pool.
choices.explanation: A connection broker is a VDI component, not a hypervisor.

questions.tip: Think about whether the virtualization layer needs an underlying general purpose OS.
questions.explanation:
Type 1 (bare metal) hypervisors install directly onto server hardware.

**Why it works:** Without an intermediate host OS, the hypervisor schedules CPU, memory, and I/O directly, giving better performance and a smaller attack surface, which is exactly what server consolidation needs.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Type 2 on Windows Server: still needs a host OS, defeating the bare metal requirement.
- Docker container runtime: shares the host kernel, it is not a hypervisor.
- VDI broker: handles session brokering, it does not virtualize hardware.

skills: 4.1: Explain virtualization concepts.
questions.question:
The operations team is rolling out a microservices application. They need each service to start in under a second, share the host Linux kernel, and be packaged with only its application binaries and dependencies, with no separate guest OS for each instance.

Which virtualization technology fits these requirements?

choices.text: Containers, which package the application and its dependencies and share the host kernel.
choices.explanation: Containers are designed for fast startup and minimal overhead by sharing the host kernel.

choices.text: Full virtual machines running on a Type 1 hypervisor, each with its own guest OS.
choices.explanation: Each VM carries a full guest OS, which is heavier and slower to start than the requirement allows.

choices.text: A VDI pool where each microservice instance is assigned a virtual desktop.
choices.explanation: VDI is for delivering user desktops, not for hosting microservices.

choices.text: Cross-platform virtualization that emulates a different CPU architecture for each service.
choices.explanation: Architecture emulation is slow and adds significant overhead, the opposite of the requirement.

questions.tip: Focus on the technology that omits a per-instance guest OS.
questions.explanation:
Containers meet the lightweight, kernel-sharing requirement.

**Why it works:** A container image only carries the application binaries and libraries, the container runtime uses kernel namespaces and cgroups to isolate processes while sharing one kernel, which gives sub-second start times.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Full VMs: each ships a guest OS, increasing image size and boot time.
- VDI pool: targets end user desktops, not service workloads.
- Cross-platform virtualization: emulates hardware, which adds overhead.

skills: 4.1: Explain virtualization concepts.
questions.question:
Following a hospital's clinical refresh, staff need to access the same Windows desktop, applications, and data from any thin client in any ward. The desktops must be centrally managed in the data centre, with no user data stored on the endpoint device.

Which virtualization solution matches this requirement?

choices.text: Virtual Desktop Infrastructure that hosts user desktops centrally and streams them to thin clients.
choices.explanation: VDI centralises desktops in the data centre and presents them remotely to endpoints.

choices.text: Installing a Type 2 hypervisor on each thin client so staff can run a local VM.
choices.explanation: Local VMs on the endpoint defeat the centralised, data-centre-only storage requirement.

choices.text: Deploying a container per user on each thin client to host their desktop session.
choices.explanation: Containers are not how full Windows desktops are delivered to end users in this pattern.

choices.text: Application virtualization that streams a single legacy app to the user's local profile.
choices.explanation: App virtualization delivers individual apps, not full roaming desktops with central data.

questions.tip: Consider which model keeps the desktop and data in the data centre, not on the endpoint.
questions.explanation:
VDI centralises desktops in the data centre.

**Why it works:** The hypervisor in the data centre hosts each user's desktop VM, a connection broker assigns the session, and the thin client only displays pixels and forwards input, so no data lives on the endpoint.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Type 2 on the thin client: stores the VM locally, not centrally.
- Per user containers on thin clients: also keep state on the endpoint and are not the standard Windows desktop delivery model.
- Application virtualization: delivers individual apps, not the whole desktop.

skills: 4.1: Explain virtualization concepts.
questions.question:
An engineer is planning a new virtualization host that will run several production VMs side by side with sensitive customer workloads. Before any VM is provisioned, they need to make sure the underlying requirements that virtualization depends on are properly addressed.

Which TWO requirements MUST be considered when planning the virtualization host?

choices.text: Sufficient storage capacity and IOPS to host the virtual disks for all planned VMs.
choices.explanation: Storage sizing and performance directly determine whether the VMs run acceptably.

choices.text: Network segmentation and bandwidth to isolate VM traffic and meet throughput needs.
choices.explanation: Networking design is a core virtualization requirement, especially when VMs share an uplink.

choices.text: Choosing a colour theme for the hypervisor management console.
choices.explanation: Cosmetic settings are not a functional virtualization requirement.

choices.text: Installing a separate desktop antivirus on the hypervisor for end user browsing.
choices.explanation: Hypervisor hosts should not be used for end user browsing, so this is not a planning requirement.

choices.text: Buying a physical KVM switch for each VM console.
choices.explanation: VM consoles are accessed through the hypervisor, not via physical KVM switches.

questions.tip: Focus on the fundamental infrastructure pillars that every VM depends on.
questions.explanation:
Storage and network are two of the three core virtualization requirements (with security).

**Why it works:** Each VM consumes disk capacity and IOPS, and shares the host's NICs, so both must be sized and segmented up front. Without enough storage performance VMs become unusable, and without proper network design tenant traffic can mix or saturate the uplink.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Management console theme: cosmetic, not a requirement.
- Desktop antivirus for browsing: hypervisors are not used as workstations.
- Physical KVM per VM: VM consoles are virtual, accessed through the hypervisor.

skills: 4.1: Explain virtualization concepts.
questions.question: Match each virtualization concept to the description that BEST fits it.

choices.text: Virtualization layer installed directly on server hardware with no underlying general purpose OS
choices.explanation: Type 1 (bare metal) hypervisors run on the hardware itself for maximum performance and a small attack surface.

choices.text: Virtualization application installed on top of an existing desktop or server operating system
choices.explanation: Type 2 (hosted) hypervisors run as an application inside a host OS, useful for labs and developer machines.

choices.text: Isolated user space package that shares the host kernel and bundles only application binaries and dependencies
choices.explanation: Containers use kernel namespaces and cgroups to share one kernel between many isolated workloads.

choices.text: Solution that hosts full user desktops in the data centre and streams them to thin clients or endpoints
choices.explanation: Virtual Desktop Infrastructure centralises desktops so endpoints only render the session.

questions.tip: Distinguish bare metal versus hosted hypervisors, and full desktop delivery versus kernel-shared isolation.
questions.explanation: Each concept differs in where the virtualization layer sits, whether a guest OS is required, and what is delivered to the user.

skills: 4.2: Summarize cloud computing concepts.
questions.question:
The marketing team at a mid-sized firm wants to use a hosted email and document suite without managing any servers, operating systems, or application patching. They simply log in through a browser and pay a monthly per-user fee.

Which cloud service model does this describe?

choices.text: Software as a Service (SaaS), where the provider manages everything below the application.
choices.explanation: SaaS delivers ready-to-use applications consumed over the network.

choices.text: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), where the customer manages the OS and applications on rented VMs.
choices.explanation: IaaS leaves OS and app management to the customer, which the team explicitly does not want.

choices.text: Platform as a Service (PaaS), where the customer deploys their own code onto a managed runtime.
choices.explanation: PaaS still requires the customer to build and deploy an application, not just consume one.

choices.text: A private cloud running on the firm's own hardware in their data centre.
choices.explanation: A private cloud means the firm operates the infrastructure themselves, not a hosted browser app.

questions.tip: Identify how much of the stack the customer is responsible for versus the provider.
questions.explanation:
SaaS is the right model when only the application is consumed.

**Why it works:** With SaaS, the provider runs the data centre, hardware, OS, and application, and the customer just signs in. That matches a monthly per-user, browser-only email and documents experience.

**Why the others don't work:**
- IaaS: hands the OS and apps to the customer to manage.
- PaaS: targets developers deploying their own code.
- Private cloud: keeps infrastructure ownership in-house, contradicting the hosted model.

skills: 4.2: Summarize cloud computing concepts.
questions.question:
During a Black Friday sale, an online retailer's web tier suddenly receives ten times its normal traffic. The cloud platform automatically adds more web server instances to handle the spike, then removes them again once traffic returns to normal.

Which cloud characteristic is being demonstrated?

choices.text: Elasticity, where resources scale up and down automatically to match demand.
choices.explanation: Elasticity is the on-demand expansion and contraction of resources in line with workload.

choices.text: Multitenancy, where multiple customers share the same underlying infrastructure.
choices.explanation: Multitenancy describes shared infrastructure between tenants, not automatic scaling for one tenant.

choices.text: File synchronization, which keeps copies of files consistent between devices.
choices.explanation: File sync is about replicating files across endpoints, unrelated to scaling web servers.

choices.text: Metered utilization, which is the per-unit billing model for cloud resources.
choices.explanation: Metering measures and bills usage but does not itself add or remove instances.

questions.tip: Look for the characteristic that ties capacity directly to fluctuating demand.
questions.explanation:
Elasticity is the cloud characteristic that grows and shrinks capacity on demand.

**Why it works:** Auto-scaling groups add instances when load rises and terminate them when load falls, so the retailer pays for capacity only while it is needed.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Multitenancy: describes shared tenancy, not dynamic capacity.
- File synchronization: replicates files between endpoints.
- Metered utilization: bills consumption but does not adjust capacity.

skills: 4.2: Summarize cloud computing concepts.
questions.question:
A regional NHS trust and three neighbouring trusts share a cloud environment built specifically to meet their common clinical, compliance, and data residency requirements. The platform is not open to the general public and is not owned by a single trust.

Which cloud deployment model does this represent?

choices.text: A community cloud shared by organisations with common requirements.
choices.explanation: Community clouds serve a defined group of organisations with shared concerns such as compliance.

choices.text: A public cloud open to any customer on the internet.
choices.explanation: A public cloud is open to anyone, which contradicts the closed, sector-specific scenario.

choices.text: A private cloud dedicated to a single organisation.
choices.explanation: A private cloud is for one organisation, but here four trusts share the environment.

choices.text: A hybrid cloud spanning on-premises and a public provider.
choices.explanation: Hybrid mixes deployment models, but the scenario describes one shared sector platform, not a mix.

questions.tip: Identify who the consumers are and whether the platform is for one organisation, several, or anyone.
questions.explanation:
A community cloud is shared by a defined set of organisations with common needs.

**Why it works:** Several trusts pool requirements, governance, and often cost on a platform that meets healthcare-specific obligations, which is the textbook community cloud pattern.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Public cloud: is open to any customer.
- Private cloud: is for a single organisation.
- Hybrid cloud: combines two or more models, which is not what is described.

skills: 4.2: Summarize cloud computing concepts.
questions.question:
After reviewing last month's cloud bill, the finance team is surprised to see a sizeable charge for data leaving the provider's network to on-premises users, while data uploaded into the cloud was free. They want to understand which cloud billing concept is in play.

Which characteristic BEST explains this charge?

choices.text: Metered utilization, specifically egress traffic billed per gigabyte leaving the provider's network.
choices.explanation: Metering with separate ingress and egress rates is standard cloud billing.

choices.text: Elasticity charges incurred when the platform scaled out web instances.
choices.explanation: Elasticity drives compute spend, not a specific outbound bandwidth line item.

choices.text: Multitenancy fees levied for sharing infrastructure with other customers.
choices.explanation: Multitenancy is a characteristic, not a billable line item.

choices.text: Availability surcharges applied because of the data centre's uptime SLA.
choices.explanation: Availability is delivered through SLAs and architecture, not as a per-gigabyte egress cost.

questions.tip: Distinguish between data flowing into the cloud and data flowing out.
questions.explanation:
Metered utilization with separate ingress and egress is the cloud's pay-as-you-go billing model.

**Why it works:** Cloud providers commonly charge for egress (data leaving the cloud) while ingress is free or cheap, which matches the bill the finance team is seeing.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Elasticity charges: relate to compute scale, not outbound bandwidth.
- Multitenancy: is an architecture trait, not a billed item.
- Availability surcharges: SLAs are not billed by the gigabyte of outbound traffic.

skills: 4.2: Summarize cloud computing concepts.
questions.question:
A small architecture practice keeps confidential project files on each designer's laptop and on the office server. They want every designer to see the latest version of a file moments after it is saved, regardless of which device they are on, and they also want a cloud copy in case a laptop is lost or stolen.

Which TWO cloud characteristics directly enable this workflow?

choices.text: File synchronization that propagates changes between endpoints through the cloud.
choices.explanation: File sync is the mechanism that keeps copies consistent across devices.

choices.text: High availability of the cloud storage service so files remain reachable from any device.
choices.explanation: Availability ensures designers can reach the synchronised copy whenever they need it.

choices.text: Dedicated single-tenant compute reserved exclusively for the practice's workloads.
choices.explanation: Dedicated compute is not what enables cross-device file consistency.

choices.text: Cloud bursting from a private cloud into a public cloud for extra capacity.
choices.explanation: Bursting addresses peak compute demand, not document synchronisation.

choices.text: Metered egress billing applied to every file download.
choices.explanation: Billing is not a feature that enables the workflow, it is a cost characteristic.

questions.tip: Focus on the cloud traits that make files appear up to date everywhere and remain accessible.
questions.explanation:
File synchronization plus availability deliver the always-current, always-reachable behaviour.

**Why it works:** Sync agents push and pull deltas through the cloud so each endpoint sees the latest version, while the cloud storage service's availability means designers can reach the file from any device at any time.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Dedicated compute: relates to isolation of workloads, not file sync.
- Cloud bursting: is about scaling compute, not propagating file changes.
- Metered egress: is a billing trait, not an enabling capability.

skills: 4.2: Summarize cloud computing concepts.
questions.question: Match each cloud service or deployment model to the description that BEST fits it.

choices.text: Provider rents virtual machines, storage, and networking, and the customer manages the OS and apps on top
choices.explanation: IaaS gives the customer the most control over the stack above the hypervisor.

choices.text: Provider delivers a managed runtime and development tools so the customer just deploys application code
choices.explanation: PaaS abstracts OS and middleware management away from developers.

choices.text: Provider delivers a finished application that users simply sign in to and consume in a browser or client
choices.explanation: SaaS is full application delivery with no customer involvement in the stack below it.

choices.text: Deployment that combines on-premises private infrastructure with one or more public cloud services
choices.explanation: Hybrid cloud blends private and public deployment models, often with orchestrated workload portability.

questions.tip: Decide how much of the stack the customer manages, and whether the deployment is mixed or single mode.
questions.explanation: The three service models differ in where provider responsibility ends and customer responsibility begins, while hybrid is a deployment pattern that crosses private and public boundaries.

skills: 5.1: Given a scenario, troubleshoot motherboards, RAM, CPUs, and power.
questions.question:
During a routine workstation refresh, a technician powers on a tower PC and hears a repeating pattern of one long beep followed by three short beeps from the motherboard speaker. The fans spin and the power LED is lit, but no image appears on the monitor.

Which component is the POST code most likely indicating has failed or is improperly seated?

choices.text: Video adapter or onboard GPU
choices.explanation: One long followed by three short beeps is a long-standing AMI/Award convention indicating a video card or display adapter failure.

choices.text: System RAM modules in the primary slot
choices.explanation: RAM failures generally produce continuous or repeating short beeps, not the one-long-three-short pattern.

choices.text: CMOS battery requiring replacement
choices.explanation: A depleted CMOS battery produces date/time errors and configuration warnings rather than a POST beep pattern.

choices.text: CPU thermal protection has triggered
choices.explanation: Thermal shutdowns cause the system to power off entirely rather than POST with a coded beep sequence.

questions.tip: Beep codes are a structured language; specific patterns map to specific subsystems.
questions.explanation:
The classic one-long, three-short beep code from AMI and Award BIOS firmware indicates a problem with the video subsystem. Reseating the GPU or testing with another card is the appropriate next step.

**Why it works:** POST runs before video is initialized, so the BIOS uses the motherboard speaker to communicate failures in a coded pattern that maps to specific hardware areas.

**Why the others don't work:**
- RAM failures: produce different beep patterns, typically repeating shorts.
- CMOS battery: causes BIOS settings loss, not POST beeps.
- Thermal shutdown: halts the system entirely rather than emitting beep codes.

skills: 5.1: Given a scenario, troubleshoot motherboards, RAM, CPUs, and power.
questions.question:
While performing preventive maintenance on a three-year-old desktop, a technician notices several small cylindrical components near the CPU socket have bulged tops with a slight crust around the seams. The user has been complaining about random reboots and the system failing to POST when cold.

Which condition is the technician observing and what is the appropriate remediation?

choices.text: Capacitor swelling on the voltage regulator stage, requiring motherboard replacement
choices.explanation: Bulged, leaking electrolytic capacitors near the CPU VRM cause unstable power delivery and indicate the board should be replaced.

choices.text: Normal thermal expansion of decoupling capacitors that can be resolved by reseating the CPU
choices.explanation: Bulging is not normal; once the can deforms, the capacitor has failed and cannot be restored.

choices.text: Dust contamination on inductors, requiring compressed air cleaning
choices.explanation: Dust does not deform component packaging; the visible bulging clearly indicates a failed capacitor.

choices.text: Flux residue from manufacturing that can be removed with isopropyl alcohol
choices.explanation: Flux residue is flat and translucent; this description matches electrolyte venting from a failed capacitor.

questions.tip: Physical deformation of a component is a definitive failure indicator.
questions.explanation:
Bulged or leaking capacitors near the CPU power circuitry are a classic failure mode that destabilizes voltage delivery and causes the symptoms described. The motherboard must be replaced.

**Why it works:** Electrolytic capacitors smooth voltage to the CPU; when they vent and bulge, ripple voltage rises and the system becomes unstable or fails to POST.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Thermal expansion: capacitors are not designed to bulge under normal use.
- Dust: does not change the shape of a component can.
- Flux residue: appears as flat film, not raised, cracked tops.

skills: 5.1: Given a scenario, troubleshoot motherboards, RAM, CPUs, and power.
questions.question:
A user complains that every time they boot their PC, the BIOS reports the system date as 1 January 2010 and Windows then warns that secure connections to websites are failing. The user has rebooted multiple times and reset the BIOS clock, but the problem returns after each power-off.

Which component should the technician replace first?

choices.text: The CMOS coin-cell battery on the motherboard
choices.explanation: A depleted CR2032 cannot maintain CMOS settings while the PSU is off, causing the clock to reset on each cold boot.

choices.text: The system RAM, which is failing to retain BIOS configuration
choices.explanation: BIOS settings are stored in CMOS, not in system RAM; RAM is not used to retain settings between power cycles.

choices.text: The power supply, which is no longer providing standby voltage
choices.explanation: Standby voltage is not what keeps the RTC running while the PSU is fully unplugged; that is the CMOS battery's role.

choices.text: The motherboard, due to a failed real-time clock crystal
choices.explanation: A failed RTC crystal would prevent timekeeping even with power applied; this scenario points to a battery that cannot hold settings between power-offs.

questions.tip: Date/time loss across power cycles points to a very specific failure.
questions.explanation:
A depleted CMOS coin cell loses the ability to keep the real-time clock running and to retain BIOS settings while the system is fully powered off, producing exactly the symptoms described.

**Why it works:** The CR2032 battery powers the RTC and CMOS NVRAM when the PSU is off; once it falls below threshold, settings revert to defaults each cold boot.

**Why the others don't work:**
- RAM: does not store BIOS settings.
- PSU standby: only present when plugged in; does not survive unplugged states.
- RTC crystal: failure produces drift while running, not a hard reset on each boot.

skills: 5.1: Given a scenario, troubleshoot motherboards, RAM, CPUs, and power.
questions.question:
Midway through a heavy compile job, a developer's workstation shuts off without warning. There is no BSOD and the event log shows no clean shutdown. After cooling for ten minutes the system boots normally, but the issue recurs whenever sustained CPU load is applied. The technician confirms that the CPU fan is spinning and the heatsink is dust free.

Which diagnostic step is MOST likely to identify the root cause?

choices.text: Reseat the CPU heatsink and reapply thermal paste, verifying full contact with the IHS
choices.explanation: Sudden shutdowns under load with a spinning, clean fan typically indicate poor heat transfer between the CPU and heatsink.

choices.text: Replace the system RAM with a known-good kit and rerun the compile workload
choices.explanation: RAM faults usually cause application crashes, BSODs, or POST failures rather than abrupt power-off only under sustained load.

choices.text: Update the network driver because heavy compilation triggers network I/O
choices.explanation: Network driver issues do not cause hard power-off events tied to thermal load.

choices.text: Disable C-states in the BIOS to prevent the CPU from entering deep sleep
choices.explanation: C-states reduce power during idle; they do not cause shutdowns under sustained load.

questions.tip: Symptom only under load and resolved by cooling time points strongly to one subsystem.
questions.explanation:
Random shutdowns triggered by sustained CPU load and resolved by allowing the CPU to cool indicate thermal protection cutting power. Reseating the heatsink and replacing dried-out thermal interface material is the standard remediation.

**Why it works:** Modern CPUs throttle, then shut down at TJ Max; dried thermal paste or a poorly mated heatsink prevents the cooler from absorbing heat fast enough.

**Why the others don't work:**
- RAM swap: would not be load-temperature correlated.
- Network driver: unrelated to thermal shutdown.
- C-state changes: address idle behaviour, not load-induced overheating.

skills: 5.1: Given a scenario, troubleshoot motherboards, RAM, CPUs, and power.
questions.question:
A help-desk technician is dispatched to a workstation that powers on briefly, runs for a few seconds, then shuts off. The cycle repeats whenever the user presses the power button. There is no POST beep, no display output, and a faint burning smell near the rear of the case.

Which TWO immediate actions should the technician take before attempting any further diagnosis?

choices.text: Disconnect the system from mains power at the wall
choices.explanation: Removing power eliminates the risk of further damage or fire from the failing component.

choices.text: Open the chassis and visually inspect for scorched components or burned capacitors
choices.explanation: A burning smell warrants visual inspection to locate the failed component before attempting any further power-on.

choices.text: Boot from a live USB to run hardware diagnostics
choices.explanation: Powering on a unit emitting a burning smell risks worsening the damage and is unsafe.

choices.text: Clear CMOS and try booting with minimum hardware installed
choices.explanation: Clearing CMOS does not address a thermal failure already producing smoke or odour.

choices.text: Swap in a known-good PSU and immediately power the system back on
choices.explanation: Acting before inspection risks damaging the replacement PSU if the fault lies on the motherboard.

questions.tip: Safety and observation come before active testing when there are signs of physical damage.
questions.explanation:
When physical signs of a hardware failure are present (burning smell, smoke, scorching), the first priority is to remove power and then inspect the system for visible damage before attempting any further testing.

**Why it works:** Disconnecting mains power prevents escalation; visual inspection identifies the failed component and avoids damaging replacement parts.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Live USB diagnostics: requires powering on a potentially unsafe system.
- CMOS clear: ignores the physical damage warning.
- Swapping PSU and powering on: may damage the replacement if the fault is elsewhere.

skills: 5.1: Given a scenario, troubleshoot motherboards, RAM, CPUs, and power.
questions.question: Match each observed symptom to the most likely failing subsystem on a desktop PC.

slots.label: System date resets to a year in the past on every cold boot
PC shuts down abruptly only during sustained CPU load
Bulged cylindrical components visible near the CPU socket
Repeating short POST beeps with no video output

choices.text: Depleted CMOS coin-cell battery
choices.explanation: The RTC and BIOS settings cannot be retained while the PSU is off without a healthy coin cell.

choices.text: CPU cooling or thermal interface failure
choices.explanation: Thermal protection cuts power when the CPU exceeds its junction temperature under load.

choices.text: Failed motherboard VRM capacitors
choices.explanation: Electrolytic capacitors that bulge or vent indicate motherboard end-of-life and require board replacement.

choices.text: Faulty or unseated system RAM
choices.explanation: Repeated short beeps in most BIOS conventions indicate a memory failure detected at POST.

questions.tip: Map each symptom to the smallest subsystem that fully explains it.
questions.explanation: Each classic hardware symptom on a desktop PC maps to a specific subsystem; recognising the pattern speeds up correct diagnosis and reduces unnecessary part swaps.

skills: 5.2: Given a scenario, troubleshoot drive and RAID issues.
questions.question:
A user reports their five-year-old desktop has become unbearably slow when opening files. The technician hears a faint rhythmic clicking from the system unit that gets louder when File Explorer is opened. Windows still boots, but file operations stall for several seconds at a time.

Which component is failing and what should the technician do first?

choices.text: The mechanical hard drive head assembly is failing; back up data immediately before replacing the drive
choices.explanation: Rhythmic clicking with stalls indicates head failure on an HDD; priority is data preservation before the drive fails completely.

choices.text: The SSD controller is failing; run TRIM and continue using the drive
choices.explanation: SSDs have no moving parts and cannot click; the symptom rules out an SSD as the source.

choices.text: The CPU fan bearing is failing; replace the cooler
choices.explanation: A failing fan produces a continuous whine or rattle that is not tied to file system activity.

choices.text: The optical drive lens is dirty; clean the disc tray
choices.explanation: The optical drive is not driven by File Explorer activity on the system disk and would not stall file operations.

questions.tip: Audible mechanical noise tied to disk activity points to one specific device class.
questions.explanation:
Clicking sounds from a hard drive, especially when correlated with file access, are a sign of imminent mechanical failure. Backing up data is the first and most important action.

**Why it works:** The read/write heads on a failing HDD repeatedly attempt to recalibrate, producing the characteristic click.

**Why the others don't work:**
- SSDs: cannot click as they contain no moving parts.
- CPU fan: noise is unrelated to file activity.
- Optical drive: not engaged during normal file operations.

skills: 5.2: Given a scenario, troubleshoot drive and RAID issues.
questions.question:
After a brief power blip in the office, a server with a four-disk RAID 5 array boots into the OS but a continuous audible alarm sounds from the chassis. The RAID controller utility shows the array status as Degraded with one drive marked Failed.

Which action should the technician take next?

choices.text: Replace the failed drive with a same-size or larger drive and initiate a rebuild from the controller
choices.explanation: RAID 5 tolerates a single disk failure; replacing the failed drive allows parity to rebuild the array.

choices.text: Power the server off immediately and reseat all four drives at once
choices.explanation: A degraded RAID 5 is still online; pulling all drives risks further corruption and is unnecessary.

choices.text: Delete and recreate the array using the remaining three drives
choices.explanation: Recreating destroys all data; the array is recoverable through rebuild.

choices.text: Convert the array to RAID 0 to improve performance while a replacement is sourced
choices.explanation: RAID 0 has no redundancy and conversion would risk total data loss.

questions.tip: Degraded RAID 5 still serves data; the goal is to restore redundancy without data loss.
questions.explanation:
RAID 5 survives a single disk failure. Replacing the failed disk and triggering a rebuild restores redundancy using parity data on the surviving disks.

**Why it works:** Parity blocks distributed across the remaining members let the controller reconstruct the missing data onto the new drive.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Power down and reseat all: unnecessary and risky.
- Recreate array: destroys data.
- Convert to RAID 0: removes all redundancy and risks loss.

skills: 5.2: Given a scenario, troubleshoot drive and RAID issues.
questions.question:
A laptop user reports that during a normal boot, the BIOS displays the message Bootable device not found. The technician confirms the SATA SSD is visible in the BIOS setup screen and reports a healthy S.M.A.R.T. status. No recent hardware changes have been made.

Which is the MOST likely cause?

choices.text: The boot loader or system partition on the drive is corrupted or missing
choices.explanation: The drive being visible with healthy S.M.A.R.T. but unbootable points to a software-level boot record issue.

choices.text: The SATA cable has come loose inside the chassis
choices.explanation: A loose cable would prevent the BIOS from detecting the drive at all.

choices.text: The SSD has failed and needs immediate replacement
choices.explanation: A failed SSD would not present a healthy S.M.A.R.T. status in BIOS.

choices.text: The CMOS battery is dead and the boot order has been lost
choices.explanation: A lost boot order would still find a bootable device if the partition is intact.

questions.tip: Distinguish between hardware visibility and software bootability.
questions.explanation:
When the BIOS sees the drive and S.M.A.R.T. is healthy but the system reports no bootable device, the most common cause is a corrupted boot sector, missing boot loader, or accidentally inactive system partition. Repair via recovery media restores boot.

**Why it works:** BIOS detection confirms the drive hardware is fine; the failure must therefore lie in the boot data on the drive.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Loose SATA cable: would prevent detection.
- Failed SSD: would show poor S.M.A.R.T.
- Dead CMOS: boot order loss alone doesn't make a healthy install unbootable.

skills: 5.2: Given a scenario, troubleshoot drive and RAID issues.
questions.question:
Following a scheduled monthly reboot, an IT admin notices the storage server displays an Array missing warning at the controller BIOS screen. The chassis LEDs show all four drives are powered and present. The admin recently swapped the RAID controller card after a hardware fault.

Which step should be taken first to recover the array?

choices.text: Use the controller's import foreign configuration option to read the existing array metadata from the disks
choices.explanation: Replacement controllers see existing arrays as foreign; importing the configuration preserves data and rebuilds the logical array.

choices.text: Initialize the disks and create a new array with the same parameters
choices.explanation: Initializing destroys the existing parity and data structures on the disks.

choices.text: Run `chkdsk` against each drive from a recovery environment
choices.explanation: `chkdsk` operates on file systems, not on RAID metadata; it cannot rebuild a missing logical array.

choices.text: Update the firmware of each individual disk to match the new controller
choices.explanation: Disk firmware updates do not address array metadata recognition by a replacement controller.

questions.tip: When a controller is replaced, the array metadata still lives on the disks.
questions.explanation:
Most modern RAID controllers store array metadata on the member disks. When the controller is replaced, importing the foreign configuration lets the new controller adopt the existing array without data loss.

**Why it works:** The disks themselves describe the array layout; the new controller just needs permission to adopt the configuration.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Initialize: wipes the existing array data.
- `chkdsk`: works on the file system after the array is online.
- Firmware updates: do not influence array recognition.

skills: 5.2: Given a scenario, troubleshoot drive and RAID issues.
questions.question:
Several users on a workstation report that file copies to and from the internal SSD have become extremely slow and that the OS occasionally freezes. The drive still appears in Device Manager and File Explorer. A technician opens the drive vendor's tool to investigate.

Which TWO indicators from the vendor tool would point to imminent drive failure?

choices.text: S.M.A.R.T. attributes show a high and increasing reallocated sector count
choices.explanation: Growing reallocated sectors indicate the drive is mapping out failing blocks and is degrading.

choices.text: Benchmark reports IOPS far below the drive's rated specification
choices.explanation: Severely degraded IOPS combined with other warnings is a strong indicator of an unhealthy drive.

choices.text: Drive temperature within the manufacturer's normal operating range
choices.explanation: Normal temperature is healthy and not indicative of failure.

choices.text: Firmware version matches the latest release available
choices.explanation: Current firmware reflects good maintenance, not impending failure.

choices.text: Power-on hours within the warranty period
choices.explanation: Being within warranty hours does not by itself indicate failure.

questions.tip: Vendor tools surface specific health attributes; look for the ones that change as a drive deteriorates.
questions.explanation:
S.M.A.R.T. reallocated sectors and degraded IOPS are concrete signs of an SSD that is no longer reliable. Both warrant prompt backup and replacement.

**Why it works:** Reallocated sectors mean the drive has run out of healthy spare blocks for some addresses; IOPS collapse reflects controller-level distress.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Normal temperature: a positive sign, not a failure signal.
- Current firmware: a maintenance state, not a health indicator.
- Power-on hours within warranty: an age metric, not a failure indicator.

skills: 5.2: Given a scenario, troubleshoot drive and RAID issues.
questions.question: Arrange the following steps in the correct order to safely replace a failed disk in a degraded hardware RAID 5 array.

choices.text: Verify backups of array data are current before any physical work begins
choices.explanation: Backups must be confirmed first in case a second drive fails during the operation.

choices.text: Identify the failed drive using the controller utility and chassis LED indicator
choices.explanation: Correctly identifying the failed disk avoids accidentally pulling a healthy member.

choices.text: Hot-swap the failed drive with a matching replacement of equal or greater capacity
choices.explanation: Hot-swap allows the array to remain online during the replacement on supported chassis.

choices.text: Initiate or confirm the automatic rebuild and monitor progress through completion
choices.explanation: Monitoring ensures the rebuild finishes and the array returns to a fully redundant state.

questions.tip: Data protection comes before hardware action; identification comes before removal.
questions.explanation: Replacing a failed RAID 5 member follows a strict order: confirm backups, identify the correct disk, hot-swap with a matching drive, then verify the rebuild completes. Skipping steps risks data loss.

skills: 5.3: Given a scenario, troubleshoot video, projector, and display issues.
questions.question:
During a board presentation, the projector image suddenly turns off while the projector fan continues to run loudly. The status indicator on the projector glows red. After about thirty minutes the unit cools and produces an image again, but the cycle repeats during use.

Which is the MOST likely cause?

choices.text: Air filter is clogged, causing the projector to overheat and trigger thermal shutdown
choices.explanation: A blocked filter restricts airflow over the lamp, raising temperature until the projector cuts off to protect itself.

choices.text: HDMI cable is partially seated, dropping the video signal
choices.explanation: A loose cable would lose signal but would not cause the projector to shut down with a red status light.

choices.text: Laptop is set to mirror displays at the wrong resolution
choices.explanation: Resolution mismatches usually show an out-of-range message, not a thermal shutdown.

choices.text: Lamp has reached end of life and needs immediate replacement
choices.explanation: An end-of-life lamp generally fails to ignite at all, rather than producing repeated overheat shutdowns.

questions.tip: Shutdowns that recover after cooling are temperature-driven.
questions.explanation:
Projectors include a thermal cut-out that disables the lamp when internal temperature exceeds safe limits. Restricted intake from a clogged filter is the most common trigger for cyclical shutdowns that recover after the unit cools.

**Why it works:** Restricted airflow raises lamp temperature past threshold; cooling cycle resets the protection until the next overheat.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Loose HDMI: drops signal, no thermal shutdown.
- Wrong resolution: produces sync errors, not shutdown.
- End-of-life lamp: usually fails to strike, not cycles by temperature.

skills: 5.3: Given a scenario, troubleshoot video, projector, and display issues.
questions.question:
A user reports that several small black spots have appeared in the same location on their LCD monitor over the past month, and that they remain visible regardless of what is being displayed. The rest of the screen behaves normally.

Which condition is the user describing?

choices.text: Dead pixels that no longer respond to image data
choices.explanation: Permanent black spots that persist across all images are the textbook definition of dead pixels.

choices.text: Burn-in from a static image being displayed too long
choices.explanation: Burn-in appears as a ghost of a prior image, not as small isolated black spots.

choices.text: Backlight failure causing localized dimming
choices.explanation: Backlight failure dims a region rather than producing discrete spots.

choices.text: Incorrect colour profile loaded by the OS
choices.explanation: Colour profiles affect tint across the whole image, not localized permanent spots.

questions.tip: Persistent, location-fixed defects across all content map to a specific defect class.
questions.explanation:
Small fixed black spots that ignore image content are dead pixels — subpixels that no longer respond to drive signals. They are a manufacturing or aging defect and not repairable in software.

**Why it works:** Each pixel is independently driven; if the driving circuit fails the cell remains in a fixed state regardless of input.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Burn-in: shows residual image, not blank spots.
- Backlight failure: produces dim regions, not pinpoint defects.
- Colour profile: applies globally, not locally.

skills: 5.3: Given a scenario, troubleshoot video, projector, and display issues.
questions.question:
After moving a desktop to a new desk, a user connects the monitor via the same HDMI cable but sees No signal on screen. The PC POSTs and the user hears the Windows login chime. The monitor's OSD shows it is set to DisplayPort.

Which action will resolve the issue most directly?

choices.text: Change the monitor's input source to HDMI
choices.explanation: The monitor is listening on a different port than the one the cable is connected to; switching input source resolves it.

choices.text: Reinstall the graphics driver on the PC
choices.explanation: Audio and POST work; the GPU is producing signal but the monitor is not listening on HDMI.

choices.text: Replace the HDMI cable with a higher bandwidth model
choices.explanation: Cable bandwidth is not the issue when the monitor is not even watching the HDMI input.

choices.text: Roll back the monitor's firmware to the previous version
choices.explanation: Firmware does not need rollback to choose an input source.

questions.tip: Check the most basic configuration step before assuming a hardware fault.
questions.explanation:
When a display shows No signal and its OSD is set to a different input than the connected cable, the fix is to select the correct input source on the monitor.

**Why it works:** Modern monitors do not always auto-detect; the user must point the panel at the active input.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Driver reinstall: PC is generating video correctly.
- Cable replacement: not a cable issue.
- Firmware rollback: input selection is a runtime setting.

skills: 5.3: Given a scenario, troubleshoot video, projector, and display issues.
questions.question:
A graphic designer reports that the image on their monitor has a noticeable red cast that has worsened gradually over several weeks. Swapping the display cable does not help, and the cast persists even at the BIOS screen on another computer.

Which is the MOST likely cause of the colour shift?

choices.text: Aging or failing backlight LEDs in the monitor
choices.explanation: When the colour shift follows the monitor across hosts and persists at BIOS, the panel itself is at fault; ageing backlight is a common cause.

choices.text: Incorrect ICC profile loaded by the design application
choices.explanation: Application profiles cannot affect the BIOS POST screen on a different computer.

choices.text: GPU output stage producing imbalanced channel voltages
choices.explanation: Swapping to another computer rules out the original GPU; the colour cast persists.

choices.text: Damaged DisplayPort cable carrying degraded colour signal
choices.explanation: The cable was already swapped without effect; cable damage has been ruled out.

questions.tip: When a symptom follows the monitor across hosts, the monitor is the suspect.
questions.explanation:
A colour cast that follows the monitor regardless of source PC or cable, and is visible even at BIOS, points to a panel-side fault such as aging backlight phosphor or LED degradation.

**Why it works:** The panel itself produces the image once it receives a signal; if it ages unevenly the white point shifts.

**Why the others don't work:**
- ICC profile: cannot affect BIOS POST.
- GPU output: ruled out by alternate PC.
- Cable: ruled out by replacement.

skills: 5.3: Given a scenario, troubleshoot video, projector, and display issues.
questions.question:
Following a desk move, a user complains that text on their external monitor is fuzzy and slightly blurred at the edges, while the same content looks crisp on the laptop's own panel. The connection between the laptop and monitor is via a VGA cable.

Which TWO actions are MOST likely to improve image clarity?

choices.text: Confirm the OS is set to the monitor's native resolution
choices.explanation: Running below native resolution causes scaling that produces fuzzy text on LCDs.

choices.text: Replace the VGA cable with a digital connection such as HDMI or DisplayPort
choices.explanation: VGA is analogue and prone to signal degradation; switching to digital eliminates fuzziness from analogue noise and termination.

choices.text: Reduce the monitor refresh rate to 30 Hz
choices.explanation: Lowering refresh rate does not improve sharpness and may introduce flicker.

choices.text: Switch the OS theme to high contrast mode
choices.explanation: Theme changes do not address the underlying signal quality.

choices.text: Disable the monitor's overdrive setting
choices.explanation: Overdrive affects pixel response time, not text sharpness.

questions.tip: Fuzziness on an LCD is usually a resolution or signal-quality problem.
questions.explanation:
Fuzzy text on an LCD is typically caused by non-native resolution scaling, analogue signal degradation, or both. Setting native resolution and using a digital connection are the two most direct fixes.

**Why it works:** LCDs are sharp only at native resolution; digital connections eliminate analogue noise inherent to VGA.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Lower refresh rate: does not affect sharpness.
- High contrast theme: cosmetic only.
- Overdrive: affects motion, not still text.

skills: 5.3: Given a scenario, troubleshoot video, projector, and display issues.
questions.question: Match each display symptom to its most likely root cause.

slots.label: A faint ghost of a previous static image visible on the panel
Monitor shows No signal while the PC has clearly POSTed
Projector shuts down after running for ten minutes and resumes after cooling
Image on monitor is dimmer than usual but still visible

choices.text: Display burn-in from a persistent static image
choices.explanation: Long exposure to unchanging content leaves a faint retained image on susceptible panels.

choices.text: Incorrect input source selected on the monitor
choices.explanation: The display is not listening on the input the cable is connected to.

choices.text: Overheating due to restricted airflow or clogged filter
choices.explanation: Thermal protection cycles the projector off until it cools.

choices.text: Failing or end-of-life backlight
choices.explanation: Backlight aging reduces luminance uniformly across the screen.

questions.tip: Tie the most distinctive aspect of each symptom to a single underlying cause.
questions.explanation: Each display symptom maps to a specific subsystem fault. Recognising the pattern allows direct remediation without unnecessary part swaps.

skills: 5.4: Given a scenario, troubleshoot common mobile device issues.
questions.question:
A user brings in a two-year-old smartphone and reports the back cover no longer sits flush against the chassis. On inspection the technician sees the back panel bulging outward in the middle of the device, and the phone runs noticeably warm even at idle.

Which action should the technician take next?

choices.text: Power the device down, isolate it from other electronics, and arrange safe battery replacement
choices.explanation: A swollen lithium-ion battery is a fire and chemical hazard; isolate and replace through proper handling.

choices.text: Apply firm pressure to reseat the back cover and continue using the device
choices.explanation: Compressing a swollen lithium-ion cell risks rupture and fire.

choices.text: Perform a full factory reset to clear background processes causing heat
choices.explanation: A factory reset cannot reverse physical battery swelling.

choices.text: Update the device firmware to improve battery management
choices.explanation: Firmware updates do not repair a physically damaged battery.

questions.tip: Physical deformation of a battery has safety priority over feature troubleshooting.
questions.explanation:
A bulging back cover almost always indicates a swollen lithium-ion battery, which is a serious safety hazard. The device should be powered down, kept away from other equipment, and the battery professionally replaced.

**Why it works:** Cell swelling indicates gas build-up inside; pressure or heat may cause venting or fire.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Pressing the cover back: risks rupture.
- Factory reset: cannot fix hardware.
- Firmware update: does not address physical damage.

skills: 5.4: Given a scenario, troubleshoot common mobile device issues.
questions.question:
A user complains their phone now drains from 100 percent to 20 percent in under three hours of light use, although the same workload lasted all day a year ago. The device does not run hot and battery health in the settings menu shows 71 percent of original capacity.

Which is the MOST appropriate remediation?

choices.text: Replace the battery, as its capacity has degraded with age and charge cycles
choices.explanation: Battery health well below 80 percent combined with rapid drain on a previously healthy device indicates wear-out, requiring replacement.

choices.text: Disable all background app refresh as the primary fix
choices.explanation: Disabling background refresh may help temporarily but does not address measured battery health degradation.

choices.text: Replace the charging cable and power adapter
choices.explanation: Cables and adapters do not affect post-charge runtime once the battery is full.

choices.text: Restore the phone to factory defaults to clear malware
choices.explanation: No malware symptoms are described; battery health is a hardware metric not changed by reset.

questions.tip: Battery health metrics give a direct hardware indicator.
