questions.explanation:
When the device's own diagnostics report degraded capacity and runtime is much shorter than when new, the battery has aged past usable life and should be replaced.

**Why it works:** Battery chemistry degrades with each charge cycle; capacity below 80 percent commonly produces the symptoms described.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Background refresh disable: addresses symptoms, not cause.
- Cable/adapter swap: irrelevant to capacity.
- Factory reset: does not change physical battery wear.

skills: 5.4: Given a scenario, troubleshoot common mobile device issues.
questions.question:
After accidentally spilling coffee on their phone, a user wiped it dry, but several hours later the screen began registering taps in locations where no finger contact was occurring. The cursor appears to drift across the screen and apps open by themselves.

Which condition is the technician most likely dealing with?

choices.text: Liquid intrusion has caused digitizer malfunction
choices.explanation: Liquid under the screen creates spurious touch signals on the capacitive digitizer.

choices.text: Screen protector has lifted and is generating phantom touches
choices.explanation: A lifted protector is mentioned nowhere; symptoms map cleanly to liquid damage.

choices.text: An OS update introduced a touch responsiveness bug
choices.explanation: Symptoms started immediately after a spill, not an update.

choices.text: The proximity sensor is misreading and triggering touch events
choices.explanation: The proximity sensor reports near/far, not coordinates; it cannot generate phantom taps across the screen.

questions.tip: Pair the timing of the symptom with the most recent event.
questions.explanation:
Liquid that reaches the digitizer layer generates false capacitive touches, producing the ghost-touch and drift behaviour described. Drying alone may not be enough; service or replacement of the screen assembly is typically required.

**Why it works:** Capacitive digitizers detect changes in capacitance; conductive liquid creates additional touch points.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Screen protector: not present in scenario.
- OS update: timing does not match.
- Proximity sensor: cannot map to touch coordinates.

skills: 5.4: Given a scenario, troubleshoot common mobile device issues.
questions.question:
A user reports that their phone takes hours to fully charge and sometimes does not detect that a cable has been plugged in. Inspecting the USB-C port with a flashlight reveals visible compacted dust and lint inside the port. The same charger works normally with a colleague's device.

Which corrective step should the technician try first?

choices.text: Carefully clear debris from the port using a wooden or plastic pick and inspect for damage
choices.explanation: Compacted lint frequently prevents proper cable seating and is the simplest fix.

choices.text: Replace the charging port assembly without further inspection
choices.explanation: Replacing the port is premature before attempting the standard cleaning step.

choices.text: Toggle airplane mode to reset charging negotiation
choices.explanation: Airplane mode does not influence physical USB charging negotiation.

choices.text: Roll back the OS to the previous version
choices.explanation: An OS rollback does not address a physical port obstruction.

questions.tip: Start with the simplest physical cause when symptoms point to the port.
questions.explanation:
Compacted lint or debris in a USB-C port is a leading cause of intermittent charging. Carefully clearing the port with a non-metallic tool often resolves the issue without further service.

**Why it works:** The cable cannot seat fully against the port pins when debris is present, so contact is lost.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Port replacement: invasive and premature.
- Airplane mode: irrelevant to physical contact.
- OS rollback: does not fix mechanical obstruction.

skills: 5.4: Given a scenario, troubleshoot common mobile device issues.
questions.question:
A user reports that their phone has become sluggish, runs warm, displays pop-up ads even when no browser is open, and shows a battery drain that doubled overnight. The user recently sideloaded an APK from a forum link.

Which TWO actions should the technician take to remediate the most likely cause?

choices.text: Boot the device into safe mode and uninstall the suspicious sideloaded application
choices.explanation: Safe mode disables third-party apps so a malicious app can be removed.

choices.text: Run a reputable mobile antimalware scan to detect any remaining threats
choices.explanation: Scanning catches associated malicious components that may have been installed by the original app.

choices.text: Disable Wi-Fi and Bluetooth permanently to stop ads
choices.explanation: Connectivity is not the cause; malware will still run locally.

choices.text: Replace the battery to address the increased drain
choices.explanation: Battery replacement does not eliminate the malware causing the drain.

choices.text: Increase screen brightness to mask the pop-up ads
choices.explanation: Brightness changes do not address malicious software.

questions.tip: Follow the symptoms back to the most recent change.
questions.explanation:
The combined symptoms and recent sideload point to malware. Safe-mode removal of the offending app followed by a scan addresses the root cause.

**Why it works:** Safe mode prevents third-party apps from loading at boot; a malware scan finds related components.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Disable connectivity: does not remove software.
- Battery swap: does not stop the malware.
- Brightness: cosmetic only.

skills: 5.4: Given a scenario, troubleshoot common mobile device issues.
questions.question: Match each reported mobile device symptom to the most likely cause.

slots.label: Back cover bulging outward and device warm at idle
Phantom taps and cursor drift after a drink spill
Cable fits loosely and charging is intermittent
Stylus inputs no longer register on a tablet

choices.text: Swollen lithium-ion battery
choices.explanation: Gas build-up inside the cell deforms the chassis and is a known safety risk.

choices.text: Liquid damage to the digitizer
choices.explanation: Conductive liquid produces spurious touch signals on the capacitive sensor.

choices.text: Lint or debris in the charging port
choices.explanation: Obstruction prevents proper seating of the connector and produces intermittent power.

choices.text: Stylus battery depleted or pairing lost
choices.explanation: Active styluses require power and association with the host device to function.

questions.tip: Each symptom has a single most likely physical cause; pair them directly.
questions.explanation: Recognising the textbook causes of mobile symptoms allows quick, low-risk remediation that preserves user data and device safety.

skills: 5.5: Given a scenario, troubleshoot network issues.
questions.question:
Several staff in a corner of the office complain that their Wi-Fi connection drops for a few seconds every five to ten minutes. Wired connections in the same room are unaffected. A site survey shows the affected area has a strong signal but a high noise floor, and a microwave oven sits in the adjacent break room.

Which is the MOST likely cause of the intermittent connectivity?

choices.text: External interference on the 2.4 GHz band from the microwave oven
choices.explanation: Microwave ovens emit strong 2.4 GHz noise that periodically corrupts Wi-Fi frames in nearby spaces.

choices.text: Wireless authentication server is rate limiting client renewals
choices.explanation: Authentication issues would generate failures across the office, not localised drops near a microwave.

choices.text: Office DHCP scope is exhausted in that area
choices.explanation: DHCP exhaustion causes a permanent inability to get an address, not periodic drops.

choices.text: VLAN trunk between the AP and switch is dropping tagged frames
choices.explanation: A trunk fault would affect the entire AP, not just users near a microwave.

questions.tip: Localised wireless drops with nearby noise sources almost always indicate interference.
questions.explanation:
Microwave ovens leak energy in the 2.4 GHz ISM band that Wi-Fi uses, producing periodic frame loss when the oven is running. Moving the AP, switching to 5 GHz, or relocating the noise source resolves it.

**Why it works:** RF interference raises the noise floor and corrupts frames; clients retransmit and may temporarily disconnect.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Auth server rate limit: would be office-wide.
- DHCP exhaustion: would be a hard failure.
- VLAN trunk: would affect all clients on the AP.

skills: 5.5: Given a scenario, troubleshoot network issues.
questions.question:
During a VoIP call between two offices, users report intermittent breaks and dropouts in audio while video conferencing remains smooth. Pinging the remote office shows average latency of 25 ms but variation between consecutive replies ranges from 3 ms to 180 ms.

Which condition is causing the audio degradation?

choices.text: High jitter is causing the VoIP buffer to underrun
choices.explanation: Voice traffic is highly sensitive to variability in packet arrival; large jitter breaks the audio stream.

choices.text: Average latency exceeds the threshold for real-time traffic
choices.explanation: An average of 25 ms is well within acceptable VoIP limits; the variability is the problem.

choices.text: Packet loss is dropping every other voice frame
choices.explanation: Packet loss is not specified; the data given describes variability rather than loss.

choices.text: MTU mismatch is fragmenting voice packets
choices.explanation: MTU issues do not produce the wide ping variation pattern described.

questions.tip: Variability in delivery times, not the average, is the key indicator here.
questions.explanation:
Jitter is the variation in packet arrival times. VoIP relies on a steady stream of small packets; high jitter causes the receiver's playout buffer to run dry, producing audible breaks. Video tolerates jitter better than voice.

**Why it works:** Voice codecs play out at fixed intervals; uneven arrivals cause underruns.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Latency average: low and acceptable.
- Packet loss: not described in the data.
- MTU mismatch: produces fragmentation, not jitter.

skills: 5.5: Given a scenario, troubleshoot network issues.
questions.question:
A network admin reviews switch logs and notices that a single access port keeps cycling its link state up and down every few seconds, generating a flood of log entries. The port serves a wall jack in a meeting room with a wired desk phone attached.

Which symptom does this describe and what is the first step to isolate it?

choices.text: Port flapping, likely caused by a faulty cable or connector; swap the patch cable and re-test
choices.explanation: Repeated link-state transitions are port flapping; a damaged cable is the most common cause.

choices.text: VLAN mismatch; reconfigure the port to access mode
choices.explanation: VLAN mismatch produces traffic loss but does not cycle the physical link state.

choices.text: MAC address table overflow on the switch; clear the CAM table
choices.explanation: CAM overflow causes flooding but not link-state oscillation.

choices.text: Spanning tree convergence; disable STP on the access port
choices.explanation: Disabling STP would worsen reliability; STP convergence does not cause continuous flapping.

questions.tip: Repeated up/down on the same port has a name and a standard first remedy.
questions.explanation:
Port flapping is the rapid up/down cycling of a switch port and is most often caused by physical layer faults — damaged cable, poor termination, or a failing transceiver. Replacing the patch cable is the first low-cost isolation step.

**Why it works:** Physical layer faults intermittently break link, triggering negotiation cycles logged as flap events.

**Why the others don't work:**
- VLAN mismatch: does not flap link.
- CAM overflow: does not affect link state.
- STP convergence: does not produce continuous oscillation.

skills: 5.5: Given a scenario, troubleshoot network issues.
questions.question:
A user reports their laptop shows a yellow exclamation mark on the network icon with the message No Internet, secured. They can reach internal file shares but cannot browse external websites. The technician runs an `ipconfig` and notes a valid private IP, subnet mask, and default gateway.

Which step should the technician check next?

choices.text: Verify the DNS server settings and test name resolution to an external domain
choices.explanation: Reachable internal resources with broken external browsing commonly indicate DNS resolution failure.

choices.text: Replace the laptop's wireless adapter
choices.explanation: Connectivity to internal shares confirms the adapter is functional.

choices.text: Re-enter the Wi-Fi pre-shared key on the laptop
choices.explanation: Re-entering the PSK is unnecessary because the laptop is already authenticated and online.

choices.text: Disable IPv6 on the wireless adapter
choices.explanation: Disabling IPv6 does not address the symptom of limited connectivity tied to name resolution.

questions.tip: Reachable internal but unreachable external usually narrows to a specific service.
questions.explanation:
Limited connectivity with internal resources reachable points to DNS or upstream routing. Testing name resolution with nslookup against an external host quickly confirms whether DNS is the issue.

**Why it works:** Browsers depend on DNS; if resolution fails, sites cannot be reached even when packets can flow.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Adapter swap: hardware is clearly working.
- Reset PSK: connection is authenticated.
- Disable IPv6: not a targeted fix for the symptom.

skills: 5.5: Given a scenario, troubleshoot network issues.
questions.question:
Throughout the day, multiple users in the same wing report slow network speeds and intermittent drops on Wi-Fi. A wired test from a laptop plugged into the same wall jack shows full link speed and stable throughput. The wireless AP in that area was recently moved to make room for a new printer cabinet.

Which TWO actions should the technician take to diagnose the wireless issue?

choices.text: Perform a site survey to measure signal strength and channel use in the affected area
choices.explanation: A survey reveals coverage gaps and channel contention introduced by the AP move.

choices.text: Review and adjust the AP channel and power settings to minimise overlap and improve coverage
choices.explanation: Re-tuning channel and power addresses interference and coverage caused by the relocation.

choices.text: Replace all client wireless adapters in the wing
choices.explanation: Multiple users sharing the same problem on different devices makes individual adapters an unlikely cause.

choices.text: Convert the AP to a wireless bridge to the printer cabinet
choices.explanation: Bridging the printer cabinet has no bearing on client connectivity.

choices.text: Disable WPA2 to reduce authentication overhead
choices.explanation: Removing encryption introduces security risk and does not address the underlying RF issue.

questions.tip: When wireless degrades but wired works, focus on the RF environment.
questions.explanation:
A site survey and channel/power tuning are the standard, low-risk steps to diagnose and improve Wi-Fi performance after coverage changes such as AP relocation.

**Why it works:** Surveys quantify the problem; channel and power tuning resolve overlap and weak coverage.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Adapter replacement: too broad given symptoms.
- Wireless bridging: unrelated to user connectivity.
- Disabling WPA2: dangerous and not the cause.

skills: 5.5: Given a scenario, troubleshoot network issues.
questions.question: Match each network symptom to the most likely underlying cause.

slots.label: VoIP audio chops while ping shows wildly varying response times
A single switch port repeatedly transitions up and down
Wi-Fi drops every few minutes only near the kitchen
Client cannot enter password correctly on a corporate SSID

choices.text: High jitter
choices.explanation: Variability in packet arrival breaks real-time audio playback.

choices.text: Port flapping due to a faulty cable or transceiver
choices.explanation: Physical layer faults trigger continuous link renegotiation.

choices.text: External RF interference from a microwave oven
choices.explanation: Microwaves emit strong 2.4 GHz noise that disrupts nearby Wi-Fi.

choices.text: Authentication failure
choices.explanation: Bad credentials or expired certificates block access to the network.

questions.tip: Symptoms map to specific layers of the network stack.
questions.explanation: Each common network symptom maps to a distinct cause; recognising the pattern lets the technician focus diagnosis on the right layer.

skills: 5.6: Given a scenario, troubleshoot printer issues.
questions.question:
A finance user complains that every page printed from their workgroup laser printer has a consistent vertical black line running from top to bottom on the right side of the page. Cleaning the page in a word processor does not help, and the line appears on test pages printed from the printer's own menu.

Which component is the MOST likely source of the defect?

choices.text: A scratched or contaminated imaging drum in the toner cartridge
choices.explanation: A line that persists on printer-generated test pages points to the toner/drum assembly rather than the source document.

choices.text: Misaligned paper tray guides
choices.explanation: Tray guides influence skew and feed, not vertical lines on the page.

choices.text: Damaged USB cable to the host computer
choices.explanation: Lines appear on internal test pages, ruling out the host connection.

choices.text: Outdated print driver on the user's PC
choices.explanation: Drivers are bypassed by the printer's internal test page.

questions.tip: Self-generated test pages remove the host and driver from the picture.
questions.explanation:
When a vertical line appears on test pages generated by the printer itself, the cause is inside the imaging path — usually a scratch or contamination on the drum. Replacing the toner/drum unit typically resolves it.

**Why it works:** Defects on the drum transfer to every page at the same horizontal position.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Tray guides: cause skew, not lines.
- USB cable: not used in self test.
- Driver: not used in self test.

skills: 5.6: Given a scenario, troubleshoot printer issues.
questions.question:
Multiple users send jobs to a shared network printer, but nothing prints. The printer is powered on, online, and shows no errors on its panel. The Windows print queue lists more than a dozen jobs in queue, all stuck at Spooling or Sending.

Which corrective action is MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Restart the Print Spooler service on the print server and clear the stuck jobs
choices.explanation: A hung spooler service is the most common cause of multiple stalled jobs and is resolved by a service restart.

choices.text: Power cycle the printer and resend each job in sequence
choices.explanation: The printer reports no errors; the problem is on the server side.

choices.text: Replace the network cable from the printer to the switch
choices.explanation: The printer is online; network connectivity is not the issue.

choices.text: Install the printer locally on each user's machine
choices.explanation: Local install bypasses the shared queue but does not fix the underlying spooler problem.

questions.tip: When the printer is fine but the queue is stuck, look at the server-side service.
questions.explanation:
A frozen print queue with many jobs and a healthy printer is almost always caused by a hung Print Spooler service. Restarting it and clearing the queue restores service.

**Why it works:** The spooler manages job submission; when it hangs, jobs accumulate without being released.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Power cycle printer: no printer error to clear.
- Cable swap: printer is online.
- Local install: workaround, not a fix.

skills: 5.6: Given a scenario, troubleshoot printer issues.
questions.question:
After a recent toner replacement, every page that comes out of a laser printer is so faded that text is barely visible. Shaking the toner cartridge does not improve density, and the printer's settings show toner level near full.

Which is the MOST likely cause?

choices.text: The sealing tape was not removed from the new toner cartridge
choices.explanation: An unremoved seal blocks toner from reaching the drum, producing very faded prints despite a full cartridge.

choices.text: Paper humidity is too high for proper fusing
choices.explanation: Humid paper causes feed problems and curling, not uniform fading.

choices.text: The toner economy mode has been enabled in the driver
choices.explanation: Economy mode produces lighter prints but not the extreme fade described after a new cartridge install.

choices.text: The fuser unit is below operating temperature
choices.explanation: A cold fuser causes smearing of unfused toner, not faded prints.

questions.tip: After a consumable change, look at the installation steps first.
questions.explanation:
Most laser toner cartridges ship with a protective seal that must be pulled out before installation. Forgetting this step produces immediate severely faded output despite a healthy cartridge.

**Why it works:** The seal prevents toner from leaving the cartridge in shipping; printing without removing it starves the drum.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Humidity: produces feed/curl issues, not fade.
- Economy mode: less dramatic effect.
- Cold fuser: produces smearing.

skills: 5.6: Given a scenario, troubleshoot printer issues.
questions.question:
An office printer repeatedly produces multipage misfeeds, pulling two or three sheets through the rollers at once and triggering jams. The paper stock is the same brand the office has used for years and the tray was recently refilled.

Which is the MOST likely root cause?

choices.text: Worn separation pad or pickup rollers no longer separating individual sheets
choices.explanation: Worn separation components cause multiple sheets to feed together; this is a normal wear item.

choices.text: Paper tray sensor incorrectly reporting tray as full
choices.explanation: A sensor fault does not cause sheets to feed in pairs.

choices.text: Outdated printer firmware that mishandles paper size
choices.explanation: Firmware does not control physical sheet separation.

choices.text: Static electricity bonding the sheets together
choices.explanation: While static can cause sticking, recurring multipage misfeeds after long reliable use are far more often due to worn separation hardware.

questions.tip: Recurring mechanical misfeeds usually trace to a consumable mechanical part.
questions.explanation:
Separation pads and pickup rollers wear with use; once worn, they no longer reliably peel one sheet off the stack, producing multipage misfeeds. Replacement returns feeding to normal.

**Why it works:** The separation pad applies friction to hold back the second sheet; when worn smooth it can no longer do so.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Tray sensor: doesn't cause double feeds.
- Firmware: not the mechanism.
- Static: less likely than worn rollers in a long-term office printer.

skills: 5.6: Given a scenario, troubleshoot printer issues.
questions.question:
Users complain that a shared network printer cannot be reached. The printer's panel shows a static IP address in the correct subnet, but pings from the print server time out. Other devices on the same VLAN are reachable.

Which TWO checks should the technician perform first to diagnose the connectivity issue?

choices.text: Inspect the printer's network cable and switch port link LED for activity
choices.explanation: A dead link LED quickly distinguishes between a cabling or port fault and a higher layer issue.

choices.text: Verify the printer's IP address, subnet mask, and default gateway are correctly configured
choices.explanation: Incorrect IP configuration is a frequent cause of an unreachable but powered printer.

choices.text: Reinstall the print driver on every workstation
choices.explanation: Driver issues do not cause ICMP timeouts from the print server.

choices.text: Replace the printer's toner cartridge
choices.explanation: Consumables do not affect network reachability.

choices.text: Reset the printer to factory defaults
choices.explanation: Factory reset clears configuration and is too drastic before basic checks.

questions.tip: Network connectivity problems are solved layer by layer, starting at the bottom.
questions.explanation:
Checking the physical link and then the IP configuration follows the standard layered approach: confirm cabling and link before inspecting layer 3 settings. Both are low-risk steps that frequently identify the cause.

**Why it works:** Layer 1 and layer 3 issues account for the majority of unreachable printers in this scenario.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Driver reinstall: not the cause of ICMP failure.
- Toner swap: unrelated to network.
- Factory reset: too aggressive before diagnosis.

Pages come out nearly blank after toner replacement

choices.text: Damaged imaging drum in the toner cartridge
